- **`is_request_too_large`** is true for a 413, a 400 whose kind is `max_tokens_exceeded`, or one whose kind is Ollaya's `INPUT_TOO_LONG` or `STATE_TRUNCATED`: the one refused body a caller fixes by sending less, state first (on Ollaya, too many options for the state's room also draw `STATE_TRUNCATED`). It reads codes, never a message.
- **A `ValidationIssue`** is an entry of the OpenAPI document's `HTTPValidationError` list. Its path runs `questions.<id>.<type>.<field>` because FastAPI puts the tag of the question's discriminated union in the location; an integer segment is kept as its decimal string.
- **The request id suffix** ` [request_id …]` is appended to a message only when there is an id; the four answer-fit errors get theirs from `Response::get`.
- **`Transport` and `ResponseTooLarge` never carry an id**: no response came back, or the loop dropped it unread with its headers, as the SDKs do.

## The observer

Token usage goes to the client's own observer when one was set on the builder and to the global one otherwise, the way `tracing` falls back to its global subscriber. Failed attempts go the same way: the retry loop takes the observer to report to, and a client passes its own or the global one. `set_global` is first-call-wins, so an application installs it once at start-up and a library never overrides it. Retried attempts are reported too. Statuses reported: an HTTP status, `transport`, `too_large`, and from the client `decode` and `unfit`; an unfit response's usage is also reported, since it was billed.

## The contract document

`contract::OPENAPI_DOCUMENT` (feature `openapi`) is the vendored TypeSafe OpenAPI 3.1.0 document, API version 0.2.0, written canonically (sorted keys, final newline) by `tests/openapi_drift.rs` so a refresh diffs cleanly. `tests/contract.rs` checks the crate against it on every run ([How the crate is checked](verification/method.md)).

## Recordings and evaluation

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    REC["recordings<br/>Recorder, or a harness by case id"] --> J["Judgment per answer and label<br/>predicted · p_expected · confidence"]
    J --> M["QuestionMetrics::summarise<br/>accuracy + Wilson 95% · Brier · ECE ·<br/>confidence when right / wrong"]
    J --> T["eval::tuning<br/>threshold sweep · gate table · level sweep"]
    T --> P["a policy: threshold, bar, bands, level<br/>written into a rubric with its provenance"]
```

**Keys.** A recording's `case` must be a name (`eval::is_name`) before `write_recording` or `read_recording` touches the file system, so an id from a document never joins a directory as a path. `request_hash` is FNV-1a 64 over a near-canonical rendering of the state and the questions, sixteen hex digits. It names recording files, so it must not move between runs, machines or toolchains, which the standard library's hasher does not promise. It stays because it names the committed recordings; the `sha256:` RFC 8785 fingerprint beside it is what a new tool computes, with the model left out. A recording also carries the server's base URL and an [RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339) timestamp, because an alias such as `jev-latest` moves. The timestamp is computed without a date dependency, through Howard Hinnant's civil-from-days algorithm.

**Grading.** A Noul is `yes` at a probability of 0.5 or more, with `max(p, 1 − p)` standing in for the confidence the wire does not send; a Choice is graded by its option keys and a Score by its level indices as strings, the most probable level predicted. An `Answer::Unknown` is graded as a miss rather than dropped, because dropping it would raise the accuracy of a model whose answers could not be read: it predicts `<kind>`, which no option key equals, with probability zero on the label and confidence zero. A label outside the option set adds the missing `(1 − 0)²` term to that judgment's Brier; unlabelled judgments count in nothing.

**Metrics.** The Brier score is the multi-class sum `Σ_i (p_i − y_i)²` against the one-hot truth, 0 perfect and 2 full confidence in the wrong option (Brier 1950); other tools halve it or report the binary form. The expected calibration error uses ten equal-width bins over the clamped confidence, `Σ_b (n_b / n) · |mean confidence_b − accuracy_b|` over the non-empty bins (Naeini, Cooper and Hauskrecht 2015). The accuracy interval is Wilson's (1927), chosen over the normal approximation because it stays inside `[0, 1]` and does not collapse to a point at 0 of 3 or 3 of 3; it assumes independent observations. Percentiles are nearest-rank. The papers are cited in [Rubrics, cases and recordings](../concepts/rubrics-cases-recordings.md#the-metrics).

**Tuning.** A threshold is a property of the model, the questions and the data together, so it is read off a table and the rule that picks from the table is printed with the result. The threshold sweep steps 0.05 to 0.95, predicts yes at `p_yes ≥ threshold`, and `best_threshold` takes the best F1 with ties to the lowest threshold, because a lower threshold says yes more often and a tie means the extra yeses cost nothing. The gate table steps a confidence bar from 0 to 0.95, reporting coverage and the accuracy among the covered; `lowest_bar` takes the lowest bar reaching a target accuracy over a minimum of covered judgments, lowest because every step up hands more work to a person. The level sweep reads a Score the way a rubric gate does, by the nearest level to the probability-weighted position rather than the most probable level, which differ on a spread distribution.

## The `.jud` reader (feature `jud`)

[The .jud format](../reference/jud-format.md) is the specification; this is how the reader applies it.

**Reading.** YAML is read with `serde_saphyr` under five options: `strict_booleans`, which keeps `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` as strings; `merge_keys = Error` and `reject_unsupported_tags`, which refuse what folds in or decodes text the reviewer did not see; `ignore_binary_tag_for_string`, which keeps a `!!binary` scalar as its text; and `with_snippet = false`, so an error names a line and a column and quotes no part of a document whose state may be someone's data. The envelope is checked first: a missing `apiVersion` or `kind` is `Missing`; an `apiVersion` that is not the string `jud/v1.3` is `Version`, naming what was found; a `kind` outside the three is `Kind`. Every kind is read through a raw struct whose keys beyond the four of the envelope are collected, and the first is refused by name, pointing at `metadata.annotations`. `metadata` is one struct for every kind; a kind then refuses by path the optional fields it does not take. Every `metadata.name` and every case `id` is checked against the name grammar before anything else about it is read. A Recording's `spec` is read as the `eval::Recording` struct with `metadata.name` inserted as its `case`. A Noul's criteria keys read through an untagged `Bool | Text` so a bare `true:` and a quoted `"true":` both land on the yes criterion. A parsed question runs through the same validation as the builder's, with a minimum of zero options when `options_from: request` and two otherwise.

**One line, every minor up to its own.** The reader reads `jud::API_VERSION` (`jud/v1`) with any `metadata.minor` up to `jud::MINOR`, refusing a higher one by number before anything else is read, and reads the earlier spelling of minor 3 (`jud/v1.3`, no `minor`) as that minor; the writer writes `jud/v1` and the minor it implements, in the order the specification states. Nothing is computed from a document's content to choose a minor, and no other envelope is read or converted. "A declaration counts by its presence" is one deserializer: a present key is `Some` whatever its value, an absent one `None`, and `null` is refused with a message that says to leave the field out.

**Why a rubric's fingerprint is its lowered request's.** A rubric question serialises as the bare wire `Question` first and adds `when`, `part_when` and `options_from` only when set, so a question without declarations is byte for byte a `Question`, and the fingerprint of a rubric's questions equals the fingerprint of the `Questions` it lowers to. A case's fingerprint covers `options`, `tags` and `note` as well as `state` and `expect`, with empty fields skipped, so adding an empty `tags` changes nothing.

**Lowering** checks the supplied options first: an id the rubric lacks, a question whose options do not come from the request, and a supplied key the static criteria already offer are each refused. Then, per question in rubric order: skip when `when` is not present; drop each instruction part whose `part_when` path is not present, and set the instructions to `null` when every part went; for a Choice with `options_from: request`, offer the supplied options in supplied order followed by the static ones; then add through the builder. `lower` and `to_yaml` re-run the checks `parse` ran, because the rubric's fields are public and a rubric built in code may never have been parsed. The order of options on the wire is witnessed by byte position in the serialised request, because `serde_json::to_value` sorts object keys while the client streams the request in insertion order.

**Applying** requires a request this rubric lowered: an id the rubric lacks or whose primitive differs is refused, the response is verified against the request, and a missing answer is the crate's `MissingAnswer`. A gate becomes bars in one place: with `bands`, one bar per band; with `confidence` only, one bar with no verdict; with neither, no bar. A bar is met with `>` when strict and `>=` otherwise. A Score's verdict uses the nearest level to the probability-weighted position. A level label resolves first as an index and then by exact text, so a level whose own text is a decimal is shadowed by the index.

**Cases.** A case's request is exactly the rubric lowered for its state with its supplied options, and both binding and grading go through it. `{from_turn: n}` keeps its key required even when `null`, so `{}` is not a label. `per_turn` resolves `from_turn` at each turn, keeps every other label only at the last turn, carries `id`, `options`, `tags` and `note` onto every turn, and returns nothing for a state that is not an array. `grade` returns one judgment per labelled question in the case's `expect` order.

## Bounded proofs

Tests check the cases someone thought of. Five pieces of arithmetic are proved for every input, or for every input within a stated bound, with [Kani](https://model-checking.github.io/kani/), a bounded model checker: the places where a float becomes an index or a length becomes a cut. Each harness is a `#[cfg(kani)]` module beside the code it proves.

| Function | Proved | Bounds and why |
|---|---|---|
| `RetryPolicy::delay_with` (`src/http.rs`) | No panic; a server wait within `retry_after_max` is returned as is; otherwise the delay is at most `backoff_max` and at most the nominal backoff, and exactly the nominal backoff without jitter | Policy durations are whole milliseconds up to one hour, or `Duration::MAX`; `retry` is 0 to 10; the server's wait and the random draw are unbounded. Unbounded durations did not finish in 40 minutes. `Duration::try_from_secs_f64` is stubbed with any result |
| `truncate_to` (`src/http.rs`) | No panic; the kept part is a prefix of the input, within the cap, on a character boundary, and less than one character short of the cap | Inputs of up to 6 bytes and caps of up to 6: every UTF-8 sequence length and every cut position occur within 6 bytes |
| `nearest_index` (`src/answer.rs`) | Always below the level count (0 with no levels), for any value including NaN and infinities; within half a level of a value on the scale | None |
| `bin_index` (`src/eval/metrics.rs`) | Always below the bin count, for any confidence including NaN, infinities and values outside `[0, 1]` | The last bin from 1 up holds for up to 2^53 bins; past that, `bins as f64` can round down. The report uses 10 |
| `nearest_rank` (`src/eval/metrics.rs`) | Always below the value count, for any `q` including NaN | The largest value at `q >= 1` holds for up to 2^53 values, for the same rounding |

Each harness carries `kani::cover!` statements, so no proof holds because its assumptions excluded every input. `mise run kani` runs all five (`cargo install --locked kani-verifier && cargo kani setup` once); it is not part of `mise run check`, because the two proofs in the HTTP module take about two minutes each.


<!-- source: docs/project/releasing.md -->


# Releasing

A release has to be the same every time: the version follows from what changed, the CHANGELOG says what the version contains, the gate has passed on exactly what is published, and the credential that publishes lives in CI rather than on a laptop. [Decision 0013](decisions/0013-releases-cut-with-cocogitto-and-published-from-ci.md) says why the pieces below were chosen over release-plz, cargo-release and a checklist. This page says how to use them.

## The pieces

| Piece | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Conventional Commits | every commit; `cog verify` in the prek `commit-msg` hook, `cog check` in the `commits` job of CI | Gives cocogitto the facts it derives a version from, and refuses a commit message it cannot read |
| `cog bump --auto` | `cog.toml`, run as `mise run release` | Computes the next version from the commits since the last tag, runs the pre-bump hooks, commits `chore(version): vX.Y.Z` and tags it |
| `scripts/release-bump.sh` | the first pre-bump hook | Writes the version into `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` and its major.minor into the README's install snippet, turns the CHANGELOG's Unreleased section into the release's dated section, and refuses an empty one |
| `cargo semver-checks check-release` | the pre-bump hook after `release-bump.sh` | Compares the public API with the latest crates.io release at the version just written: a breaking change under a patch bump fails before the gate and the commit; under a minor bump it passes (0.x). Needs the network and `cargo-semver-checks` (`mise install`) |
| `scripts/record_demo.sh` | the second pre-bump hook | Records the command-line demo again as `docs/demo.cast`, from the example recordings with no network, so the version the cast shows is the one being released |
| The gate | the remaining pre-bump hooks, then CI on the pull request and on the tag | Formatting, clippy, the no-`http` build, the tests, rustdoc, the documentation checks and what the package would ship; in CI also the `semver`, `deny`, `msrv` and `hack` jobs ([Contributing](contributing.md#the-gates)) |
| `.github/workflows/release.yml` | on a pushed `v*` tag | Runs the CI gate on the tagged commit, builds, checks and packages the `jud` binary for each platform ([The jud command line](../reference/cli.md)), checks the tag against `Cargo.toml`, runs `cargo publish --dry-run`, publishes, and creates a GitHub release with the CHANGELOG section as notes and the tarballs with `SHA256SUMS` as assets. A `workflow_dispatch` is a dry run that builds every leg and publishes nothing |
| `scripts/image-context.sh` and the `Dockerfile` | the `image` job of the release workflow, after the publish | Fills the image's build context from the two Linux tarballs the release carries, builds `ghcr.io/chussenot/jud` for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, runs the runner's platform (version, a document read, a keyless run, a replay) and pushes the image tagged `X.Y.Z`, `X.Y` and `latest` with a build-provenance attestation. On a dry run it builds and runs, and pushes nothing |
| `scripts/homebrew-formula.sh` | the `homebrew` job of the release workflow, after the publish | Renders the Homebrew formula for `jud` from the release's checksums and commits it to [chussenot/homebrew-tap](https://github.com/chussenot/homebrew-tap) as `jud X.Y.Z`, so `brew install chussenot/tap/jud` serves the release. The tap's own CI audits, installs and tests what was committed. On a dry run the formula is rendered and printed, not committed |

The CHANGELOG stays hand-written, in [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/) form: a pull request that changes what a consumer sees adds its entry under Unreleased, and the bump only dates that section. cocogitto's own changelog generation is off, because a list of commit subjects does not explain a change to a consumer.

## What the commits decide

cocogitto reads the commits since the latest tag. Below 1.0, as the crate is:

| Commits since the last tag | Next version |
|---|---|
| Any `feat`, or any commit with `!` after its type or a `BREAKING CHANGE` footer | minor: `0.2.0` to `0.3.0` |
| Only `fix` (and types that bump nothing) | patch: `0.2.0` to `0.2.1` |
| Only `docs`, `chore`, `ci`, `test`, `refactor`, `style`, `build`, `perf` | no release; `cog bump` says so and does nothing |

A breaking change in a 0.x crate is a minor bump, which is the rule the CHANGELOG states; from 1.0 on, cocogitto makes it a major. Merge commits are ignored. `mise run release:dry` prints the version the commits call for without touching anything.

## Cutting a release

1. Be on an up-to-date `main` with a clean tree. Check that the CHANGELOG's Unreleased section says what the release contains; a release with an empty section is refused.
2. `mise run release:dry` to see the version. If it is not the one the changes warrant, the commits say something the changes do not; fix that first (an amended message on an unmerged branch, or a further commit), never the version by hand.
3. `git switch -c release/vX.Y.Z` with that version, then `mise run release`. cocogitto runs the pre-bump hooks (the version into the three files, then the gate), commits `chore(version): vX.Y.Z` and tags `vX.Y.Z` on that commit. A failed hook leaves the tree edited and nothing committed; `git checkout .` restores it.
4. Push the branch and open a pull request. CI runs the gate and the commit check on it like any other change.
5. Merge it with a merge commit. Never squash or rebase this pull request: the tag points at the bump commit, and `main` has to carry that very commit for the tag to be a commit on `main`.
6. `git push origin vX.Y.Z`, one tag per push. The release workflow runs: the gate once more, the three binary legs, the version check, the dry run, the publish, the GitHub release with the binaries attached. The crate is on crates.io and `mise use -g github:chussenot/judgment@latest` resolves the version when the `publish` job is green; `brew install chussenot/tap/jud` serves it when the `homebrew` job is green and the tap's CI has passed on its commit; `ghcr.io/chussenot/jud:X.Y.Z` pulls when the `image` job is green.

Agents working in the repository cannot do steps 3 and 6 by accident: the Bash guard denies `cargo publish` (the dry run is allowed) and pushing a tag.

## One-time setup

- **The baseline tag.** cocogitto scans from the latest tag because the history before this repository was not written to the convention. Tag the commit that released 0.2.0 and push the tag; its tree has no release workflow, so nothing runs:

  ```sh
  git tag -a v0.2.0 9ccd761 -m "judgment 0.2.0"
  git push origin v0.2.0
  ```

- **The first publish** (done: 0.3.0, 2026-10-03). crates.io lets a trusted publisher be configured only on a crate that already exists, so the first release used an API token with the `publish-new` and `publish-update` scopes, stored as the `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` secret of the `crates-io` environment. crates.io also requires a verified email address on the publishing account; without one the upload is refused with a 400 and the job is re-run once the address is verified.
- **Trusted publishing, now that the crate exists.** On the crate's settings page on crates.io, add a trusted publisher: GitHub, owner `chussenot`, repository `judgment`, workflow `release.yml`, environment `crates-io`. Then delete the `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` secret: the workflow exchanges its OIDC identity for a token that lives for the job and is revoked at its end. That path has not run yet; watch the first release that uses it.
- **The environment.** Put required reviewers on the `crates-io` environment to have a person approve each publish, and restrict it to tags matching `v*`.
- **The Homebrew tap.** The `homebrew` job pushes to [chussenot/homebrew-tap](https://github.com/chussenot/homebrew-tap) with the `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` repository secret: a fine-grained personal access token whose only repository is the tap and whose only permission is Contents, read and write, with an expiry, renewed when it lapses. Without the secret the job fails after the publish, with a message, and is re-run once the secret exists.
- **The container image.** The `image` job pushes to `ghcr.io/chussenot/jud` with the job's own token (`packages: write`), so no secret is needed. The first push creates the package as private: on its settings page on GitHub, make it public and link it to this repository (the `org.opencontainers.image.source` label does the linking on later pushes). Pulls need no account once it is public.
- **Merge method.** Disable squash merging and rebase merging in the repository settings, or take care on the release pull request (step 5 above).
- **Locally.** `mise install` builds `cog` from crates.io (a cloud session downloads its release binary); `mise run setup` installs the hooks, the `commit-msg` one included; `mise run commits:check` is what CI runs on a pull request.

## When something goes wrong

- **The commit check fails on a pull request.** Reword the commit on the branch and force-push the branch; the message, not the code, is what failed.
- **`cog bump` refuses to run.** It wants a clean tree on `main` or a `release/*` branch and a non-empty Unreleased section; its message says which.
- **A binary leg fails.** Nothing was published, crates.io included: the publish job needs every leg, so a version whose binary does not build on one platform is not released. The leg's log says which platform and why; fix the cause on `main` through a pull request and retag as below. `workflow_dispatch` on the fixed branch builds every leg without publishing, which is the way to try a pipeline change before a tag.
- **The release workflow fails before `cargo publish`.** Nothing was published, and the version is still the one `main` carries, so there is nothing to bump again (the bump script refuses a manifest that is already past the latest tag). Fix the cause on `main` through a pull request, move the tag to the fixed head and push it again: `git tag -f vX.Y.Z origin/main && git push --force origin vX.Y.Z`. The workflow's checks hold on any commit that carries the version. Never move a tag once the publish step has run: the version is on crates.io and the tag must keep naming what was published.
- **`cargo publish` succeeded and a later step failed.** The version is on crates.io and cannot be re-published. Re-run the failed job for the GitHub release; do not retag.
- **The `image` job failed.** The release is complete; only the image is behind. The check step ran the image on the runner before any push, so a failure there is a real one in the Dockerfile or the context script and is fixed on `main` and re-run; a failure in the push is the registry or the package's permissions (one-time setup). Re-run the job: it rebuilds from the same tarballs and pushes the same tags. An image pushed under `latest` by a later re-run of an older tag's job would move `latest` backwards; re-run only the newest release's job, or retag by hand with `docker buildx imagetools create`.
- **The `homebrew` job failed.** The release is complete; only the tap is behind. Fix the cause (usually the token: expired, or missing) and re-run the job; it renders the formula from the same tarballs and commits only if the tap does not already carry the version. By hand, with the release's `SHA256SUMS` downloaded: `scripts/homebrew-formula.sh X.Y.Z SHA256SUMS > Formula/jud.rb` in a checkout of the tap, committed as `jud X.Y.Z`.
- **A published version is wrong.** `cargo yank --version X.Y.Z` by hand, from a machine with a token, hides it from new resolutions; a yank is not a deletion and is recorded in the CHANGELOG under the version. The fix is the next release.


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/method.md -->


# How the crate is checked

The unit and integration tests never leave the process: wiremock for the client, `Fake` and recordings for everything else. That keeps the gate fast and free, and it means the gate cannot tell whether a server speaks the wire the way the mocks assume. Three further checks can, each answering a different question. The records of what they found are the other pages under [Verification](hosted-typesafe.md).

## Does a real server speak the wire this way?

`tests/live.rs` holds twenty-one `#[ignore]` tests (one more with the `multipart` feature, and one more with `zstd`, which `live:typesafe` turns on) that run the three text primitives, an image with a Box question about it, a body compressed with zstd against the same body plain, the same image as a shared array and as a multipart part (on `jev-preview` against the hosted API, chosen while `jev-latest` was Jev 1.13; both aliases point to `jev-1.14.0` as of 2026-10-25), a state over the default budget under long context, the bodies themselves against the published document, a structured Score level (and print how the server echoes it), the model list, an unknown model name, an unknown extra body field, the server's own limits, the stability of repeated calls, the confidence formulas, the token budget, a bearer check and a record-then-replay against whatever `JUDGMENT_LIVE_BASE_URL` points at. `cargo test` skips them. Eight tasks run them:

| Task | Against | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `mise run live:typesafe` | the hosted API, `jev-latest` by default | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in `.env`; spends a handful of model calls |
| `mise run live:openrouter` | Jev through OpenRouter's System One API, base URL `https://openrouter.ai/api` (or `OPENROUTER_BASE_URL`), `jev-latest` by default | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in `.env`; spends a handful of model calls, billed to the OpenRouter account |
| `mise run live:liquid` | Liquid's System One API, base URL `https://api.liquid.ai/decisions` (or `LIQUID_BASE_URL`), `d1` by default (`LIQUID_MODEL`) | `LIQUID_API_KEY` in `.env`; spends a handful of model calls, billed to the Liquid account |
| `mise run live:laya` | `laya-serve` on `LAYA_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:8000`) | a running server; [the Laya record](laya-typed-decisions.md) says how to start one |
| `mise run live:ollama` | Ollama's `/v1/systemone` on `OLLAMA_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:11434`) with `tev1:0.8b`, or `OLLAMA_MODEL=clef` or `clef-flash` for Cloudflare's models | Ollama 0.35 or later and `ollama pull tev1:0.8b`; that model runs on a CPU, Clef wants a GPU (0.35.1 for `ollama pull clef`) |
| `mise run live:ollaya` | Ollaya's TypeSafe-compatible API on `OLLAYA_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:11435`) with `laya:en`, or `OLLAYA_MODEL` | Ollaya 0.17 or later (`ollaya serve`, `ollaya pull laya:en`); runs on a CPU; [the Ollaya record](ollaya.md) says how to install it |
| `mise run live:pplx` | Perplexity's [pplx-decider-v1.1-27b](https://huggingface.co/perplexity-ai/pplx-decider-v1.1-27b) through the `autojev-serve` its checkpoint ships, on `PPLX_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:8010`), model `autojev-qwen3.8-27b` by default | a CUDA GPU with about 49 GiB for the weights; the snapshot's `source/` installed with its `requirements.txt`, then `AUTOJEV_CHECKPOINT=<snapshot> PORT=8010 autojev-serve`. `PPLX_API_KEY` when the server sets `AUTOJEV_API_KEY`, which also runs the bearer test |
| `mise run live:clef` | Cloudflare's Clef on Workers AI through `tools/systemone/serve.py`, `clef` by default and `CLEF_MODEL=clef-flash` for the 9B | `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` and `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` in `.env`; spends a handful of model calls |

Servers that speak the wire still differ where the contract is silent: the status of a refusal, the limits, the token budget. `JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE` names the server, and each task sets its own (`typesafe`, `laya`, `autojev`, `openrouter`, `liquid`, `ollaya`, `generic` for Ollama and Clef; an exported value wins). A difference is asserted on the profile it was observed on and printed on the others, so a server's next release that changes one fails its own run, and a new server is a new profile rather than a test that guesses. The model name is not used for this: `autojev-serve` answers to `jev-latest` too, and was once held to the hosted API's status codes because of it. Unset, the profile is `generic`, which prints every outcome and asserts only what every server owes the crate; against the hosted API an unset profile stops the run instead, since its pins are what a run there is for. What each profile pins is on its server's page: [the hosted API](hosted-typesafe.md) and [its Jev 1.14 run](hosted-typesafe-jev-1-14.md), [Laya](laya-typed-decisions.md), [autojev-serve](autojev-serve.md), [Liquid](liquid.md), [Ollaya](ollaya.md).

Every body a test reads as sent, a success, a refusal or the model list, is also checked against the vendored OpenAPI document (below), and the verdict printed: which component it was held to, and every field that fails, down to the answer kind's own branch. The client decodes into types that tolerate more than the document allows, so a server can pass every other test and still send what the contract does not; this is where that shows. A status the document does not list (only 200 and 422 are) is named as such: the hosted API's 400 and laya-serve's 413 are refusals the client handles, not bodies the document describes. A success body that fails the document fails the run on the profiles that hold their server to it, `typesafe`, `autojev`, `liquid` and `ollaya`; on the others it is reported, until a run shows the server holds.

A run that passes, or that finds a departure, becomes a page under `docs/project/verification/` naming the server, its release and the date. None of these runs in CI: the gate stays offline, and a key in CI would be a secret the repository does not need.

## Does it hold at scale?

`examples/typed_decisions.rs` replays the [typed-decisions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions) benchmark (400 cases, 2,000 typed decisions) through the crate and scores it with `judgment::eval`, live or from recordings. `examples/typed-decisions/` holds a 40-case sample and `tools/typed-decisions/export.py` exports the full split. The example is a compatibility test at scale before it is an evaluation: every combination of primitive and criteria shape the benchmark uses goes through the builder, the client and the decoder. It was run against Laya's `typed-decisions` checkpoint, and the decoding bug it caught is in [the Laya record](laya-typed-decisions.md#the-bug-the-run-caught). `tools/systemone/serve.py` serves the wire over open-weight models that do not serve it at the standard path themselves: Laya in this process, for when `laya-serve` is not wanted and as the one Laya server that answers `GET /v1/models`, and Cloudflare's Clef on Workers AI, which takes the body at one URL per model inside Cloudflare's envelope.

## Does the crate match the published contract?

TypeSafe publishes an OpenAPI document for the System One API at <https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json>. A copy is vendored at `tests/fixtures/typesafe-openapi.json` (OpenAPI 3.1.0, API version 0.2.0), and `tests/contract.rs` validates against it as JSON Schema 2020-12, offline and in every `cargo test`:

- every request shape the builders produce (each primitive, string, object, array and null instructions, one-sided and structured Noul criteria, undescribed options, 255 options, 2 and 10 levels of every level shape), sent through each client entry point, with the method, path, content type and bearer scheme the document names, and also against a closed copy of the request components, so a renamed or misspelt field fails even where the published schema, which closes no object, would take it as an extra key;
- every response a `Fake` builds, and all 40 committed recordings under `examples/recordings/typed_decisions`, as committed and after a decode and re-serialise;
- the document's own examples, which decode through `Response` and read through typed handles, and its model list and validation error, through `list_models` and `Error::InvalidRequest`.

Where the crate and the schema disagree the test pins the difference, each at its own path, so a refreshed document that closes one fails loudly:

- **The crate sends what the schema refuses**: a null or numeric state, an empty question set. The client takes any `Serialize` state and the builder does not refuse an empty `Questions`, so such a request reaches the server, which is expected to refuse it with a 422. Numeric instructions, a boolean Noul criterion and a numeric Score level are not on the list: the builders refuse them as the schema does (`Error::InvalidQuestion`).
- **The builder refuses what the schema allows**: 1 option, 1 level, an empty question id, an empty option key. It follows the HTTP API reference page, which is stricter than the schema. Until 2026-10-25 the schema allowed 256 options and 11 levels as well; the document of that date bounds them (`maxProperties: 255`, `maxItems: 10`), and the hosted API now refuses them from its schema with a 422. It was probed past those limits on 2026-10-03, when it refused 256 options and 11 levels with a 400, refuses an empty question id with a 400, and answers one option or one level with probability 1 and accepts an empty option key, so the upper bounds are the server's and the lower ones this crate's alone (the rustdoc of `question` says why).
- **The crate decodes differently**: it refuses a probability or confidence outside `[0, 1]` and a negative token count, which the schema types as bare numbers, because a value no threshold can use is better an error; and it accepts a response without `usage`, with `usage` or a token count null, with no answers, or with a legend entry that is null or a scalar, which the schema refuses, because decoding is tolerant and `Response::verify` is what holds a response to its questions. A `Fake` asked nothing answers `answers: {}`, which the schema refuses.

An answer of a kind the document does not name decodes as `Answer::Unknown` and is refused by the schema. That case is not run through the validator: one test compares the document's discriminator mappings with the crate's kinds, so a document that adds a kind fails there.

An application that validates its own traffic against the same document reads it as `judgment::contract::OPENAPI_DOCUMENT` with the `openapi` feature, so its checks and the crate's cannot drift apart.

### Refreshing the copy

The copy is refreshed only through `tests/openapi_drift.rs`, an ignored test that needs the network and no key. It compares the copy with the live document and names what differs; with `JUDGMENT_OPENAPI_WRITE` set it rewrites the copy canonically instead:

```sh
cargo test --test openapi_drift -- --ignored          # stale?
JUDGMENT_OPENAPI_WRITE=1 cargo test --test openapi_drift -- --ignored
cargo test --test contract                            # review the refresh
```

A refreshed document is a contract change: `tests/contract.rs`, the CHANGELOG and the README's guarantees move together, and the committed recordings must still replay.

## What each check cannot establish

The live tests show that one server, on one day, accepted and answered what the crate sends; they say nothing about accuracy on your data. The benchmark shows the decoder and the metrics on real answers; it is one checkpoint on the task it was tuned for. The contract test checks the published schema, not a live account: a server can accept or refuse what its schema does not say, which is what the live tests are for. What all three leave open is calibration on your own questions, which only labelled history replayed through `judgment::eval` can measure ([Testing without the model](../../guides/record-replay-and-test.md)).


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/hosted-typesafe.md -->


# Against the hosted TypeSafe API

The [judgment crate](../../../README.md) is tested against mocks of TypeSafe's wire and the vendored OpenAPI document. A mock and a schema both encode what someone believed about the wire; only the server can contradict that belief. The [Laya run](laya-typed-decisions.md) checked the crate against a second implementation of System One, but no TypeSafe key was available then, so the hosted API itself had answered this client only once, through a set of triage questions (2026-09-23). That run proved those questions round-trip; it did not exercise the crate's edges: structured Score levels, null option descriptions, an unknown extra field, the model list, a wrong key.

This page records the run that did. All ten tests in `tests/live.rs`, the same file the Laya run used, passed against `https://api.typesafe.ai` with a real key on 2026-10-03; five more, written from the probes [below](#beyond-the-test-file), passed the same day. `mise run live:typesafe` runs them all under the `typesafe` profile, with a sixteenth added since, which holds every success body to the published document ([How the crate is checked](method.md)), and two more for an image with a Box question and for long context, run on 2026-10-15 against Jev 1.14.0 ([Jev 1.14 on the hosted API](hosted-typesafe-jev-1-14.md)).

## What was tested, and with what

| | |
|---|---|
| Server | `https://api.typesafe.ai`, the crate's default base URL |
| Key | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, from the environment |
| Model requested | `jev-latest`, the crate's default; it resolved to `jev-1.13.0`, the version the 2026-09-23 run saw |
| Crate | `judgment` at the commit this page was added in, built with its default `http` feature |
| Tests | `tests/live.rs`, all ten, with `--test-threads=1`; the bearer test pointed at the same server with the same key |

Total wall time was about four seconds for the nine tests that call the model: the hosted API answers in hundreds of milliseconds, against two seconds per case for Laya on CPU, so the crate's 10 s default timeout is the right default for it. The run spends a handful of model calls on the account.

## What the hosted API does

What each test asserts and why it exists is tabled on the [Laya page](laya-typed-decisions.md#the-tests); this is what the hosted API showed on each point, set against what Laya did where they differ.

- **The three primitives round-trip through their typed handles.** The out-of-domain probe, a customer whose payouts have failed for three days, went to `Billing` with probability 0.91 and confidence 0.86, urgency 0.91, severity 1.99 on a three-level line (`blocked`). Laya's fine-tuned checkpoint sent the same message to `technical` at 0.45. The judgment is sensible as well as well-formed, which no mock can show.
- **No undocumented top-level fields.** `Response::extra` was empty: the hosted response is exactly the documented shape. Laya adds `routing`.
- **A request id comes back.** The response carries one (`req_…`), on success and on the 401 and 400 below. Laya sends none.
- **The model alias resolves and says to what.** `jev-latest` was answered by `jev-1.13.0`, named in `Response::model`. On Laya the model name routes silently and `model` is the same for every checkpoint.
- **`GET /v1/models` is served.** It listed `jev-latest` and `jev-preview`. Laya answers 404, so a consumer that lists models has something to list on the hosted API and nothing on Laya.
- **Structured Score levels are echoed verbatim.** The object level came back as a JSON object, the array level as a JSON array, the string as a string, and `Response::verify` passed. Laya did the same through 0.3.21; `laya-serve` 0.3.22 and later echo the JSON text they showed the model instead ([the Laya record](laya-typed-decisions.md#re-run-against-laya-serve-0324)), which is why `verify` now compares a structured level by what the echo parses to rather than by its text.
- **A Choice option without a description is accepted**, as TypeSafe documents.
- **An unknown extra field is refused, not answered.** A request with an unknown `CallOptions::extra` field got a 400, decoded as `Error::InvalidRequest`, with the message `Invalid request.` and an empty `issues` list; only the request id identifies the call. Laya answered the same request. The crate sends extra fields as given and leaves the choice to the server, so both outcomes pass, but a caller adding a field the API does not know gets no hint which field was wrong.
- **A wrong key is a 401, classified as `Error::Unauthorized` and not retried; the right key is answered.**
- **The builder's limits hold without a request** (255 options, at least two levels, no null level); this test needs no server and is listed for completeness.

## Beyond the test file

The ten tests send what the builder lets through. On 2026-10-03 the hosted API was also probed with what the builder refuses, and with repeats, to learn what the schema and the reference page do not say (about fifty requests, sequential, far under the account's 80 requests and 100,000 input tokens per second). What held, and what the crate did with it:

| Probe | What the hosted API did | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 256 options; 11 levels | `400 {"detail": "Too many choices. Must have at most 255 choices."}`, and the same sentence for levels | The builder's upper bounds are the server's. The rustdoc of `question` said this was unobserved; it now says what was observed, and a live test pins it |
| 0 options; 0 levels | `400 {"detail": "Choice question must have at least one choice: c"}`; `422` with a `too_short` issue at `questions.s.score.criteria` | Two shapes for one kind of mistake: hand-written checks answer a 400 with a sentence, the schema's own a 422 with issues |
| 1 option; 1 level | Answered: probability 1, confidence 1 | Accepted upstream, decides nothing; the builder's minimum of 2 is the crate's choice alone, and the docs now say so |
| A `null` level | `422`, three issues for the one value, one per type the field accepts (`criteria.1.str`, `criteria.1.dict[any,any]`, `criteria.1.list[any]`) | A union-typed field yields one issue per alternative with a trailing type segment; `ValidationIssue` keeps the path as sent, and its docs say to expect this |
| Unknown model; `JEV-LATEST` | `400 {"detail": {"error_type": "api_usage_error", "message": "Unknown model: …"}}` | A third 400 shape, undocumented: an object with a code and a message. Model names are case-sensitive |
| An extra top-level field | `400 api_usage_error`, message `Invalid request.`, naming no field | `CallOptions::extra` cannot be used against the hosted API; the live test records the refusal |
| An extra field inside a question | Answered, the field silently ignored | A misspelt optional field (`instruction`) is dropped without a word, which is the case for a typed builder over a hand-written map |
| A state of about 40,000 tokens | `400 {"detail": {"error_type": "max_tokens_exceeded"}}`, no message | The one 400 whose remedy is a smaller state. `Error::InvalidRequest` now carries the code as `kind`, `Error::is_request_too_large` names it (as it names the 413 `laya-serve` answers for the same reason), and the detail reads `max_tokens_exceeded` rather than the raw body |
| No `Authorization` header; a `Basic` scheme | `403 {"detail": {"error_type": "authentication_error", "message": "Must supply an API key! …"}}`; a wrong key is the `401` the test covers | The crate cannot send no key, but a proxy that strips the header shows as `PermissionDenied` with that message; its docs say so |
| Empty question id | `400 {"detail": "Question key cannot be empty."}` | The builder refuses it before sending |
| Two questions with the same id in the raw JSON | Answered: the last one, silently | The server keeps the last duplicate; the builder's `DuplicateQuestionId` is what stands between a caller and a question that vanishes |
| Option keys `""`, `a.b`, `1`, `Billing` beside `billing` | All accepted and given probability; case distinguishes keys | The builder now refuses the empty key, which could come back as the `choice`; the rest pass through |
| `state` as a string, an array, a number, `null` | String and array answered, as documented; a number is a `422` with three issues (`state.str`, `state.dict[any,any]`, `state.list[any]`); `null` is `missing` | `Client::system_one` takes any `Serialize`; what it must serialise to is a string, an object or an array |
| `GET /v1/models` | Lists `jev-latest` and `jev-preview`, both resolving to `jev-1.13.0`; `release_date` is an RFC 3339 timestamp with microseconds, not the `YYYY-MM-DD` of the OpenAPI document; the versioned name is not listed but is accepted in a request | `fixtures/models.json` is now this list; `ModelInfo::release_date` stays a string. To pin a version, read `Response::model`, not the list |
| The same request repeated: a clear-cut one three times, twice over, then three voice commands six times each | The chosen option and the nearest level held in every repeat. On the clear-cut request, probabilities 0.01 apart in one set and 0.05 in the next (confidence 0.89, 0.83, 0.90); on a saturated one (`What's my current balance?`, p 1.00) no movement over six; on two ambiguous commands the top probability moved by 0.19 (0.65 to 0.84) and 0.12, and the confidence by 0.28 (0.48 to 0.76) and 0.17 | **Not deterministic, and the spread grows with ambiguity.** A recording is one draw; a threshold near an observed value flips between runs, and the less clear the input, the wider the band it flips in; a test must not assert a live probability to the hundredth. A live test pins the stable part (the decision) and prints the spread |
| Confidence against the documented formulas | Choice: `(p_max − 1/n)/(1 − 1/n)` within 0.01 of the wire in every case; Score: `score` equals `Σ i·p_i` exactly, confidence within 0.015 | `Choice::confidence_from_probabilities`, `Score::expected_value` and `Score::confidence_from_probabilities` compute them, so a caller can see at once whether a server (Laya) defines confidence otherwise |
| Options reversed | `billing` 0.94 against 0.92–0.93 in the original order | Within the run-to-run spread on a case this clear; the known-issues page's order bias is real but needs an uncertain case to measure. A caller that compares runs keeps its option order stable |
| Headers | `x-typesafe-request-id` on the 200 and on every 4xx; no rate-limit or `Retry-After` header seen (no 429 was provoked); served through Cloudflare | What the crate reads is what is sent |
| Load and cost | p50 250 ms per request; 25 Nouls in one request in 344 ms for 820 input tokens; ten mixed questions in 229 ms. Output tokens scale with the answer (about 20 per Noul, 17 per Score, 24 plus 6 per option for a Choice; 2,826 for 255 options) and are free | Batching is nearly free in latency; a Choice over many options is a flat distribution (top probability 0.05 over 255), which is the documented reason for hierarchical selection |

The OpenAPI drift test ran the same day: the vendored document is the live one, so every contract pin above describes the current server.

## What this does and does not establish

It establishes that the crate's wire matches the hosted API on every edge the live tests cover, with no change to the crate. Together with the 2026-09-23 triage run, it means both the crate's general surface and a set of production triage questions have been answered by Jev at least once.

It does not establish anything about thresholds or accuracy on your own questions: that needs labelled history replayed through `judgment::eval`. And `jev-latest` is an alias. When it moves past `jev-1.13.0`, the answers these tests and the committed recordings saw may change without any code changing; pin the model once thresholds are tuned, and repeat this run when the alias moves.

## Repeating the run

```sh
mise run live:typesafe
```

The task needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` (from `.env`, which mise loads) and fails before building anything when it is unset. It points both the live tests and the bearer test at `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` (default `https://api.typesafe.ai`) with that key, and asks for `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` (default `jev-latest`). It is not part of `mise run check` and never runs in CI: the gate stays offline, and a key in CI would be a secret the repository does not need.

Without mise, the same run is:

```sh
JUDGMENT_LIVE_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai JUDGMENT_LIVE_API_KEY="$TYPESAFE_API_KEY" \
JUDGMENT_LIVE_AUTH_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai JUDGMENT_LIVE_AUTH_API_KEY="$TYPESAFE_API_KEY" \
JUDGMENT_LIVE_MODEL=jev-latest JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE=typesafe \
  cargo test -p judgment --test live -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
```


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/hosted-typesafe-jev-1-14.md -->


# Jev 1.14 on the hosted API, images and the Box

[The earlier record](hosted-typesafe.md) verified the three text primitives against the hosted API on `jev-1.13.0`. Jev 1.13 also takes images, and Jev 1.14 adds the Box, a question that locates something in one. The crate's support for both ([decision 0024](../decisions/0024-images-are-part-of-the-request.md), the `.jud` format's minor 4) was written against the published pages and the refreshed OpenAPI document, and then run against the server on 2026-10-15 with a real key. This page records that run.

## What was tested, and with what

| | |
|---|---|
| Server | `https://api.typesafe.ai` |
| Model requested | `jev-preview`, which resolved to `jev-1.14.0`; `jev-latest` was still `jev-1.13.0` |
| Crate | `judgment` at the commit this page was added in, with the `http` and `jud` features |
| Live tests | `an_image_and_a_box_question_round_trip` in `tests/live.rs`, under the `typesafe` profile: a 320 by 320 PNG through `Client::answer_with_assets` with a Noul and a Box, then the same body raw with and without the images header, each body held to the OpenAPI document; `a_state_over_the_default_budget_is_answered_with_long_context`, the budget test's state with the long-context header |
| Recording run | `jud record` over the forty shapes cases, committed under `examples/recordings/shapes/` ([the calibration study](box-calibration-study.md)) |
| Probes | about twenty raw requests past what the client lets through: the image at five sizes and as a JPEG, dimensions outside the limits, an unreferenced asset, a Box with no image, with `null` instructions, with criteria, a wrong `format`, a Box on `jev-latest`, an image on `jev-latest` |

## What the hosted API does

- **An image round-trips, and the Box answers inside it.** `jev-1.14.0` put the circle of `shape-01.png` at an overlap of 0.96 with the box the generator drew it at, confidence 0.82, with `circle_present` at 0.99. The body the client sends, `assets` under the state with the base64 and the format and the header `typesafe-danger-zone-images: true`, is the body the document describes, and the success body conforms to `SystemOneResponse` with the `box` answer kind.
- **The header is required, and its absence is a 400 that says so.** `api_usage_error`, "Images are experimental. Send the header TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true to use them." The client sets the header on every request that carries an image or asks a Box, so a caller never sees this.
- **Images work on Jev 1.13; the Box needs 1.14.** A Noul about an image was answered by `jev-1.13.0` under `jev-latest` (863 input tokens, the image counted); a Box under `jev-latest` is a 400 `api_usage_error` with the message "Invalid request." and nothing naming the question type. The crate's Box documentation names `jev-preview` until the alias moves.
- **The dimension limits are a 400, not a 413.** A side under 256 or over 1568, or more than 2,458,624 pixels, is `api_usage_error`, "Invalid image dimensions."; the [Images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/images) page files size limits under 413, which the probes could not reach: a PNG inside the pixel limits is a few megabytes, far under the 16 MiB file limit. The crate checks the dimensions and the 78,400 pixel minimum (which rules out 256 by 256) before anything is sent, as `Error::InvalidImage`, so the 400 is never paid for; the 413 mapping stays for the size limits, untested.
- **An unreferenced asset is refused**, 400 `api_usage_error`, "Invalid image request.", whether it is the only asset or one of two. The client refuses it first, by the reference's name (`Error::InvalidAsset`).
- **A Box without an image is answered**, with a box over nothing at confidence 0.03. The reference page says a Box locates something in an image; the server does not insist on one. The crate sends such a request as written (a rubric's image may come with the case, or `jud RUBRIC --asset`), and the gate catches the answer: this is the strongest reason the Box documentation pairs it with a Noul.
- **`null` instructions and `criteria` on a Box are accepted** and the criteria ignored; a PNG declared `format: jpg` is accepted and sniffed. The crate refuses all three before the wire, since none can mean what the caller meant: the instructions are all a Box is, a Box has no outcomes to describe, and a format that is not the bytes' is a mistake somewhere.
- **Long context lifts the budget on Jev 1.13 as the page says.** The 40,000-token state the budget test sends, refused without the header as 400 `max_tokens_exceeded`, was answered under `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true` by `jev-1.13.0` in 1.4 s, 74,550 input tokens counted (the eighteenth live test). The crate sends the header through `CallOptions::long_context` and `ClientBuilder::long_context` ([decision 0027](../decisions/0027-long-context-is-a-switch-on-the-call.md)).
- **Input tokens follow the pixels**: 860 at 320 by 320, 2,400 at 640, 5,760 at 1024, 12,828 at 1568, for the same twenty output tokens and a latency between 190 and 300 ms. [The calibration study](box-calibration-study.md) tables it.

## What the crate changed for it

Nothing in the wire shape, which the OpenAPI refresh of the same day had already settled. Two things in words: the format page no longer says a reader must refuse a Box in a rubric without an image, and the Box's documentation names which alias answers it. The two live tests are the seventeenth and eighteenth in `tests/live.rs`; `mise run live:typesafe` runs them with the others, asking `jev-preview` for the Box part until `jev-latest` is 1.14.

## Re-checked on 2026-10-25

Four images about a filled circle, one Noul each, sent as `jev-latest` with the images header. The aliases have moved and the smallest side has risen:

- **`jev-latest` is Jev 1.14.** Every answer named `jev-1.14.0`, the model this page had to request as `jev-preview` on 2026-10-15.
- **The smallest side is now 280, as the [Images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/images) page says.** 280 by 280 and 280 by 400 were answered (0.98 and 0.97); 279 by 400, 256 by 400 and 400 by 256 were refused with the same 400 as above, `api_usage_error`, "Invalid image dimensions.". The record above shows only that a side under 256 was refused on 2026-10-15, the 256 the crate has used since; `asset::MIN_SIDE_PX` moves to 280, so the crate refuses those images before the wire again.
- **The option and level bounds moved into the schema.** The OpenAPI document of the same day bounds a Choice's `criteria` at 255 and a Score's at 10, and the hosted API refuses 256 options or 11 levels with a 422 from that schema ("Dictionary should have at most 255 items", "List should have at most 10 items") where it sent a 400 on 2026-10-03; one option and one level are still answered. The vendored document was refreshed and `tests/contract.rs` follows it.
- **The live suite passes on `jev-latest`.** `mise run live:typesafe`: nineteen of nineteen, the Box among them, with the `jev-preview` special case gone.

## Multipart, later the same day

The document's second request body, `multipart/form-data`, was then implemented behind the `multipart` feature ([decision 0028](../decisions/0028-multipart-is-a-feature-and-a-switch.md)) and sent to the hosted API with the same shapes image and the same two questions: a `request` part holding the JSON body with the asset as `{type: image, part: part-0}`, and the PNG as `part-0` under `image/png`. `jev-1.14.0` answered in 0.7 s with a box at an overlap of 0.98 with the label, at the same 1,167 input tokens as the base64 body for the same request; two raw sends of each form, through `curl`, gave the same tokens every time and boxes within 0.01 of each other, so the transport changes neither the cost nor the answer. The nineteenth live test, `an_image_goes_as_a_multipart_part_too`, runs under the feature.

## Compressed bodies, 2026-10-25

The client's opt-in zstd body ([decision 0029](../decisions/0029-request-compression-is-a-feature-and-a-switch.md), which cites the API's rules) was sent to the hosted API by `a_zstd_body_is_read_as_the_json_it_holds`: the same request of about 1.8 KB plain, then compressed at level 3. `jev-1.14.0` answered both, with 566 input tokens each and `urgent` at 0.94 each, so the server read the compressed bytes as the JSON they hold. `mise run live:typesafe` runs the test, since the task turns the `zstd` feature on. Not established: gzip, which the crate does not send; a window near the 8 MiB the API allows (level 3 stays under 2 MiB); the `415` path; and any compatible server, none of which has been sent a compressed body.


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/box-calibration-study.md -->


# A Box calibration study on synthetic shapes

[The .jud format](../../reference/jud-format.md) grades a Box by intersection over union against a labelled box ([decision 0026](../decisions/0026-a-box-is-graded-by-intersection-over-union.md)) and reports the confidence the model gives beside it. Whether the two numbers mean anything, and what a gate on the confidence buys, is a question for recordings, not for a page. This is the first such run: small, synthetic and committed, so that it replays with no key, and so that the next run has a baseline to be set against. [The second run](box-calibration-study-pages.md), on generated document pages with a stamp a tenth of the page wide among a logo, a signature and a barcode, is set against it.

## What was run

| | |
|---|---|
| Images | `examples/jud/images/shape-00.png` to `shape-39.png`: forty 320 by 320 PNGs drawn with Pillow from one seed, each a flat background with, in thirty of them, one filled circle of random size, colour and position and one distractor square; in ten, squares only. The generator's own coordinates are the labels, so no labeller's judgment is in them. |
| Rubric | `examples/jud/shapes.jud`: `circle_present`, a Noul with its two criteria, and `circle`, a Box asking for the filled circle in `image`; the policy gates the Noul at 0.5 and the Box at a confidence of 0.5 |
| Cases | `examples/jud/shapes-cases.jud`: forty cases, each naming its image by a path relative to the document and labelled `true` with the circle's box, or `false` with no box |
| Server, model | `https://api.typesafe.ai`, `jev-preview`, answered by `jev-1.14.0` |
| Run | `jud record examples/jud/shapes.jud examples/jud/shapes-cases.jud --out examples/recordings/shapes` on 2026-10-15; forty requests in about seven seconds, 93 to 532 ms each, median 119 ms, 625 input tokens and 37 output tokens a request |
| Report | `jud eval examples/jud/shapes.jud examples/jud/shapes-cases.jud --replay examples/recordings/shapes`, replayed in `tests/jud.rs`, which pins the counts below |

## The Noul: forty of forty, calibrated

| | |
|---|---|
| Labelled, right | 40, 40 (accuracy 1.00, 95 % interval 0.91 to 1.00) |
| Brier score, calibration error | 0.001, 0.015 |
| Probability of yes | 0.99 or 1.00 on every image with a circle; 0.03 or 0.04 on every image without |
| Gate at 0.5 | acts on 40, defers 0, accuracy when acted 1.00 |

A filled circle on a flat background is the easiest question the model can be asked, and it answers it as a calibrated model should: the probability sits at the ends, and the ten negatives are as confidently no as the thirty positives are yes. The number to carry forward is not the accuracy but the Brier score: on a target this clean, 0.001 is the floor a harder set is measured from.

## The Box: twenty-eight of thirty at the 0.5 bar

| | |
|---|---|
| Labelled, right | 30, 28 (accuracy 0.93, 95 % interval 0.79 to 0.98) |
| Mean intersection over union | 0.80 |
| Confidence when right, when wrong | 0.75, 0.49 |
| Calibration error, over the confidence against hits | 0.21 |
| Brier score | none: a Box has no distribution to score |

Where the overlap fell, with the model's mean confidence in each band:

| Intersection over union | Cases | Mean confidence | Which |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0 up to 0.5 | 2 | 0.49 | 00, 10 |
| 0.5 up to 0.7 | 2 | 0.86 | 06, 34 |
| 0.7 up to 0.8 | 4 | 0.73 | 18, 22, 36, 37 |
| 0.8 up to 0.9 | 14 | 0.73 | 05, 08, 09, 12, 14, 16, 17, 21, 24, 28, 29, 30, 32, 33 |
| 0.9 to 1.0 | 8 | 0.77 | 01, 02, 04, 13, 20, 25, 26, 38 |

The two misses are worth reading. `shape-00` (overlap 0.00, confidence 0.29) is the case where the model took the circle's rows and the distractor square's columns: the box spans the circle's height at the square's position, a box over nothing. `shape-10` (overlap 0.24, confidence 0.70) is a box on the right circle, too large on one side. The first is the kind of miss a confidence gate catches and the second is the kind it does not: at the 0.5 bar the gate defers the first and acts on the second.

## Confidence against the overlap

| Confidence | Cases | Right at 0.5 | Mean overlap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0 up to 0.3 | 3 | 2 | 0.58 |
| 0.3 up to 0.5 | 4 | 4 | 0.83 |
| 0.5 up to 0.7 | 2 | 2 | 0.80 |
| 0.7 up to 0.9 | 12 | 11 | 0.79 |
| 0.9 to 1.0 | 9 | 9 | 0.86 |

On the ten images with no circle, the Box's confidence was 0.02 to 0.04: the box it returns there (it always returns one) comes with a confidence that says, by itself, that there was nothing to find. In this set the Box's confidence alone separates present from absent as cleanly as the Noul does; a harder set may not, and the rubric keeps the Noul beside the Box because the format's rule is that the Box answers where, never whether.

What the policy's gate at 0.5 does with the forty answers: it acts on 23 (22 right, accuracy when acted 0.96) and defers 17: the ten empty images, one miss and 6 hits the model was unsure of (overlap 0.77 to 0.92 at confidence 0.27 to 0.48). The calibration error of 0.21 is the model's under-confidence on those: it was right at 0.3 to 0.5 more often than the number says. A caller that pads a deferred box and crops anyway loses little here; one that asks again on a larger crop spends a call on an answer that was already right in six cases of seven. `jud tune` would move the bar down on these recordings; the rubric's note says the bar is a starting point, and thirty cases are too few to move it on.

## Scale against latency, tokens and the box

The same image, `shape-01.png`, sent raw at five sizes and as a JPEG, with the same Box question, one request each:

| Image | Bytes | Status | Latency (ms) | Input tokens | Overlap with the label | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256x256 png | 1294 | 400 | 424 | - | - | - |
| 320x320 png | 1645 | 200 | 194 | 860 | 0.93 | 0.81 |
| 640x640 png | 3232 | 200 | 234 | 2400 | 0.93 | 0.82 |
| 1024x1024 png | 6130 | 200 | 221 | 5760 | 0.92 | 0.69 |
| 1568x1568 png | 11676 | 200 | 298 | 12828 | 0.91 | 0.69 |
| 320x320 jpg q90 | 5530 | 200 | 196 | 860 | 0.95 | 0.80 |

Input tokens grow with the pixels, about one token per 120 pixels at 320 by 320 and one per 190 at 1568 by 1568, so the largest image costs fifteen times the smallest; latency barely moves, since the answer is twenty tokens whatever the image. The box is as good at 320 as at 1568 on a target this large, and the confidence falls as the image grows. 256 by 256 is refused: each side is at the minimum but the product, 65,536 pixels, is under the 78,400 the API requires, which the crate's `Image` checks before anything is sent. The one PNG that stays within the pixel limits is at most a few megabytes, so the 16 MiB file limit and the 32 MiB request limit cannot be reached with a valid image; nothing was sent that would have been a 413.

## What the hosted API refused, and what it did not

| Request | Status | Body |
|---|---|---|
| A side under 256, a side over 1568, more than 2,458,624 pixels | 400 | `api_usage_error`, "Invalid image dimensions." |
| An asset nothing in the state or the questions refers to | 400 | `api_usage_error`, "Invalid image request." |
| An image without the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images` header | 400 | `api_usage_error`, "Images are experimental. Send the header …" |
| A Box on `jev-latest` (Jev 1.13.0) | 400 | `api_usage_error`, "Invalid request." |
| A Box with no image in the request | 200 | a box over nothing at confidence 0.03 |
| A Box with `instructions: null` | 200 | a box, at confidence 0.75 |
| A Box with `criteria` | 200 | the criteria ignored |
| A PNG declared `format: jpg` | 200 | the bytes sniffed |
| An image referenced by a Noul alone, on `jev-latest` | 200 | answered by `jev-1.13.0` |

The crate refuses before the wire what the API refuses (the dimensions, the missing reference), and also what the API lets through but cannot mean anything (`null` instructions, criteria on a Box, a format that is not the bytes'); it sends a Box without an image, since the image may come with the request, and the gate catches the answer. [Jev 1.14 on the hosted API](hosted-typesafe-jev-1-14.md) is the verification record these probes belong to.

## What to take from it, and what not

- A Box on a clear target is accurate at the 0.5 bar and its overlap is high (0.80 on average); the bar is a floor, not a target, and a crop that needs the box tight sets `iou_at_least` higher in the label.
- The confidence is informative in both directions: near zero when there is nothing, and lower on the boxes that were off. It is under-confident in the middle here, and `jud eval`'s calibration error is the number to watch when the target gets harder.
- Send the smallest image that keeps the target legible: the tokens are the cost, the latency is not, and the box did not improve with size.
- Thirty labelled boxes give an interval of 0.79 to 0.98 on the accuracy: wide. The set is a baseline and a regression check (`tests/jud.rs` fails if a re-recording changes the counts), not a measurement of the model.

To repeat it against the live API: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in `.env`, `model: jev-preview` in `jud`'s configuration file ([Configuration](../../reference/configuration.md)), then the `jud record` line above with `--refresh` into a scratch directory, and `jud eval` with `--replay` pointed at it. To regenerate the images, the generator is Pillow drawing from a fixed seed, which is why the labels are exact; the committed PNGs are the ones the recordings were made on, and a redrawn set changes every request fingerprint.


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/box-calibration-study-pages.md -->


# A Box calibration study on document pages

[The first study](box-calibration-study.md) asked Jev 1.14 for a filled circle on a flat background: a target a sixth to a half of the image wide, with nothing else round in it. It ended with the questions a harder set should answer: how the overlap falls on a small target, whether the confidence still tracks the overlap, what the gate's accuracy becomes when it acts, and whether the under-confidence it found between 0.3 and 0.5 holds. This is that run, on something closer to a document a service would crop: a generated invoice with a round ink stamp a tenth of the page wide, over printed text, among three things that are round, inked or black and are not a stamp. The pages are drawn, not photographed, for the same reason the shapes were: the generator's coordinates are the labels, the set regenerates from one seed, and nothing in it belongs to anyone.

## What was run

| | |
|---|---|
| Pages | `examples/jud/images/page-00.png` to `page-39.png`: forty 600 by 780 pixel pages drawn by `scripts/gen-document-pages.py` from one seed, each an invoice, delivery note, purchase order or receipt with a round two-letter logo in the header, two address blocks, a table of five to nine lines, a totals block, a signature scribble and a barcode. Thirty carry one stamp: two rings with a word (`RECEIVED`, `PAID`, …) and a date inside, 48 to 72 pixels across (median 60, 8 to 12 % of the width, under 1 % of the area), rotated up to 28°, in red, blue, green or purple ink at 78 % opacity, anywhere under the header, text and table included; ten carry none. Saved with a 64-colour palette: 12 to 15 KB each. |
| Rubric | `examples/jud/stamps.jud`: `stamp_present`, a Noul whose `false` criterion names the logo, the signature, the barcode and the table as not a stamp, and `stamp`, a Box asking for the round ink stamp on `page`; the policy is the shapes rubric's, a threshold of 0.5 on the Noul and a confidence of 0.5 on the Box, so the two studies compare |
| Cases | `examples/jud/stamps-cases.jud`, written by the generator: forty cases, each naming its page by a path relative to the document and labelled `true` with the stamp's bounding box (the outer ring's, which a rotation keeps), or `false` with no box |
| Server, model | `https://api.typesafe.ai`, `jev-preview`, answered by `jev-1.14.0` |
| Run | `jud record examples/jud/stamps.jud examples/jud/stamps-cases.jud --out examples/recordings/stamps` on 2026-10-15, with `model: jev-preview` in the configuration file; forty requests in six seconds, 114 to 678 ms each, median 124 ms, 1,596 input tokens and 37 output tokens a request |
| A second size | the same forty pages drawn at scale 2 (1200 by 1560 pixels, every coordinate doubled, so the labels in fractions are the same) and recorded the same way into a scratch directory, not committed: 161 to 644 ms, median 179 ms, 5,180 input tokens a request |
| Report | `jud eval … --replay examples/recordings/stamps`, replayed in `tests/jud.rs`, which pins the counts below; the per-case tables come from the recordings' boxes against the cases' labels |

## The Noul: forty of forty at both sizes

| | 600 by 780 | 1200 by 1560 |
|---|---|---|
| Labelled, right | 40, 40 (accuracy 1.00, 95 % interval 0.91 to 1.00) | 40, 40 |
| Brier score, calibration error | 0.007, 0.040 | 0.001, 0.020 |
| Probability of yes, with a stamp | 0.75 to 0.99 (one page at 0.75, the next at 0.89) | 0.98 to 0.99 |
| Probability of yes, without | 0.05 to 0.08 | 0.04 to 0.06 |
| Gate at 0.5 | acts on 40, defers 0, right on 40 | the same |

A stamp over text among a logo, a signature and a barcode is a harder question than a circle on a flat background, and the Noul answers it as well: not one of the ten pages without a stamp got more than 0.08, with the round logo in every header. `jud tune` proposes a threshold of 0.10 on these recordings, because every bar from 0.10 to 0.75 is forty of forty and ties go to the lower one; that is the tie rule speaking, not evidence, and the bar stays at 0.5.

## The Box: twenty-four of thirty at the 0.5 bar, thirty of thirty at twice the pixels

| | 600 by 780 | 1200 by 1560 | Shapes, 320 by 320 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Labelled, right at 0.5 | 30, 24 (accuracy 0.80, 95 % interval 0.63 to 0.90) | 30, 30 (1.00, 0.89 to 1.00) | 30, 28 (0.93) |
| Mean intersection over union, median | 0.65, 0.64 | 0.70, 0.71 | 0.80 |
| Confidence when right, when wrong | 0.81, 0.81 | 0.86, none wrong | 0.75, 0.49 |
| Calibration error, over the confidence against hits | 0.096, over-confident | 0.137, under-confident | 0.21, under-confident |
| Target's width, as a share of the image's | 8 to 12 % | 8 to 12 % | 16 to 48 % |
| Input tokens a request | 1,596 | 5,180 | 625 |

Where the overlap fell, with the model's mean confidence in each band:

| Intersection over union | Pages at 600 by 780 | Mean confidence | Which | At 1200 by 1560 | Mean confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0 up to 0.5 | 6 | 0.81 | 09, 23, 31, 33, 34, 37 | 0 | |
| 0.5 up to 0.7 | 12 | 0.75 | 00, 01, 03, 04, 10, 13, 19, 20, 21, 27, 35, 38 | 14 | 0.83 |
| 0.7 up to 0.8 | 10 | 0.87 | 07, 11, 14, 16, 17, 22, 25, 26, 28, 39 | 10 | 0.87 |
| 0.8 up to 0.9 | 2 | 0.86 | 06, 12 | 6 | 0.93 |
| 0.9 to 1.0 | 0 | | | 0 | |

The first thing the small target changes is the shape of the distribution. On the shapes it ran from 0.00 to 0.98, with two misses that were a box over nothing and a box too large on one side; here it runs from 0.45 to 0.85, every box on the stamp and none tight. The six misses are all at 0.45 to 0.49, a hair under the bar, and they look alike:

| Page | Overlap | Confidence | The stamp (label) | The box the model gave | Its centre against the stamp's |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 09 | 0.46 | 0.85 | 48 by 48 px | 36 by 47 px | 9 px left, 10 px down |
| 23 | 0.46 | 0.86 | 72 by 72 | 90 by 62 | 2 px left, 20 px down |
| 31 | 0.49 | 0.94 | 62 by 62 | 90 by 39 | 12 px left, 2 px down |
| 33 | 0.45 | 0.78 | 64 by 64 | 90 by 47 | 13 px left, 15 px down |
| 34 | 0.45 | 0.87 | 70 by 70 | 84 by 62 | 3 px right, 21 px down |
| 37 | 0.49 | 0.59 | 66 by 66 | 78 by 70 | 3 px left, 19 px down |

Five of the six boxes are wider than the ring and shorter than it, as if the model boxed the word across the stamp's middle rather than the ring around it, and five sit 10 to 21 pixels low. On a 60-pixel target a 15-pixel shift alone takes a box of the right size from an overlap of 1.0 to 0.6. Over all thirty, the box covers 82 % of the stamp's area on average (54 % at worst) and 76 % of the box is stamp; a service that pads the box before cropping gets the whole stamp in 20 of 30 crops at a quarter of the box's size each side and in 29 of 30 at half, and at the larger size in 29 and 30 of 30. The 0.5 bar measures the box's precision, not whether the stamp was found: it was found on every page.

## Confidence against the overlap, and against nothing

| Confidence | Pages at 600 by 780 | Right at 0.5 | Mean overlap | At 1200 by 1560 | Right | Mean overlap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0 up to 0.3 | 0 | | | 0 | | |
| 0.3 up to 0.5 | 1 | 1 | 0.64 | 0 | | |
| 0.5 up to 0.7 | 4 | 3 | 0.58 | 1 | 1 | 0.66 |
| 0.7 up to 0.9 | 15 | 11 | 0.63 | 17 | 17 | 0.65 |
| 0.9 to 1.0 | 10 | 9 | 0.69 | 12 | 12 | 0.78 |

The confidence does not tell a near miss from a hit here: 0.81 on average for both, with the worst-overlapping box (page 33) at 0.78 and the box that missed by the least margin in shape (page 31) at 0.94. The under-confidence the first study found between 0.3 and 0.5 cannot be tested on these pages: one answer fell in that band, none at the larger size. On a document the model is sure of its box whether or not the box is tight, and at the larger size slightly more sure of boxes that are tighter (0.78 mean overlap in the top band against 0.65 below it), which is as much relation as there is.

What it says about presence is the finding of this run. On the ten pages with no stamp, the Box put its box on the round logo in the header every time, at a confidence of 0.36 to 0.54 at the smaller size and 0.49 to 0.59 at the larger: over the gate's bar on three pages of ten, then on nine. On the shapes it had given 0.02 to 0.04 on an empty image, and the first study allowed that a harder set might not; this one does not. Once something on the page resembles the target, the Box's confidence stops saying whether the target is there, and a rubric that read the Box alone would crop a logo. The Noul beside it, at 0.05 to 0.08 on the same pages, is what keeps that from happening, which is the format's rule ([Visual judgments](../../concepts/visual-judgments.md)): the Box answers where, never whether.

What the gate at 0.5 does with the forty answers, at 600 by 780: it acts on 32 (29 stamps, of which 23 at or over the bar, and 3 logos) and defers 8 (7 empty pages and one stamp, whose box was right); accuracy when acted 0.79 over the boxes, where the shapes gate was right on 22 of the 23 it acted on. At 1200 by 1560 it acts on 39, every stamp right and nine logos with them. `jud tune`, which sweeps the bar over the labelled boxes, finds no bar that reaches 95 % accuracy over three cases at the smaller size (accuracy sits at 0.79 to 0.81 from a bar of 0 to 0.80, with coverage falling) and leaves the confidence as written; at the larger size it proposes 0, since every labelled box is right with no bar, and says so. Neither sweep sees the logos: a page with no stamp has no box label, so the pages the bar should defer are not in the table the bar is read from. A proposal of 0 for a Box means the labelled boxes are good, not that the gate is needless.

## Resolution, for a small target

The first study sent one image at five sizes and found the box as good at 320 pixels as at 1568, for a target a third of the image wide. On a target a tenth of the page wide, twice the pixels did something:

| | 600 by 780 | 1200 by 1560 |
|---|---|---|
| Stamp, in pixels | 48 to 72 | 96 to 144 |
| Right at the 0.5 bar | 24 of 30 | 30 of 30 |
| Mean overlap | 0.65 | 0.70 |
| The six misses | 0.45 to 0.49 | 0.51 to 0.83 (page 09 from 0.46 to 0.83) |
| Pages whose overlap fell | | 11 of 30 (page 12 from 0.85 to 0.70, 17 from 0.73 to 0.58) |
| Best overlap | 0.85 | 0.88 |
| Input tokens, latency (median) | 1,596, 124 ms | 5,180, 179 ms |

More pixels raised the floor and left the ceiling: no box got tight, the near misses became hits, and a third of the pages lost some overlap. The price is 3.2 times the tokens for 55 ms, so the rule the first study gave stands with a number on it: send the smallest image that keeps the target legible, where legible for a Box means about a hundred pixels across. A page whose stamps are smaller than that is better cropped first, by the Noul's page and a coarse box, then asked again on the crop, than sent whole at the API's largest size.

## What to take from it, and what not

- On a small target the misses are near misses: every box was on the stamp, at an overlap of 0.45 to 0.85. A `iou_at_least` of 0.5 in a label says how tight the application needs the box, not whether the model can find the thing; label it at what the crop needs.
- The Box's confidence is not a presence signal once the page holds something round: 0.4 to 0.6 on a logo, 0.8 on a stamp. Gate on the Noul first, as the format asks, and read the Box's confidence as a measure of the box, which here it barely is.
- Pad before cropping: a quarter of the box each side contained the whole stamp in two crops of three, half of it in all but one. A tight box wants a second call on the crop.
- Pixels buy accuracy on a small target and nothing on a large one; about a hundred pixels across is where the near misses turned into hits here, at three times the tokens.
- `jud tune` sweeps labelled boxes; pages without the target are not in its table. Read a Box proposal as a statement about the boxes it saw.
- Thirty stamps give an interval of 0.63 to 0.90 on the accuracy, and the ten empty pages all carry the same logo in the same corner: a second distractor at another position is the next thing to add. The set is a baseline and a regression check (`tests/jud.rs` fails if a re-recording changes the counts), not a measurement of the model.
