To repeat it against the live API: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in `.env`, `model: jev-preview` in `jud`'s configuration file ([Configuration](../../reference/configuration.md)), then the `jud record` line above with `--refresh` into a scratch directory and `jud eval` with `--replay` pointed at it. `python3 -I scripts/gen-document-pages.py --out DIR --scale 2` draws the larger set with its cases document; a page drawn with another Pillow or another font is other bytes, so the committed pages are the ones the recordings answer, and a redrawn set is a new run.


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/pairwise-judge-position-and-tone.md -->


# Position and tone bias of Jev 1.13 and 1.14

[arXiv 2610.18122](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18122) (Lukassen, Weisser and Silbersdorff, 2026) found that every typed decision model it tested changed verdicts when two answers swapped places, and that rewriting the better answer in an emotional tone hurt them most. This page runs the two tests on the pinned Jev versions the hosted API served on 2026-10-18, with the commands of [Test a judge for position and tone bias](../../guides/test-a-judge-for-position-and-tone-bias.md). It is one small set, not a replication of the paper.

| | |
|---|---|
| Date | 2026-10-18 |
| Models | `jev-1.13.0` and `jev-1.14.0`, requested by version, each response naming the version that answered |
| Rubric | `examples/jud/pairwise-judge.jud`: one Choice, the two answers as its options |
| Cases | `examples/jud/pairwise-judge-cases.jud`: 50 pairs of LLMBar's Natural set (Zeng et al., ICLR 2024, MIT), the 25 shortest with the better answer first and the 25 shortest with it second |
| Tone rewrites | `examples/jud/pairwise-judge-tone.yaml`: each better answer kept and put in one of CALM's four tones in turn, 13 cheerful, 13 sad, 12 angry, 12 fearful; written for this example |
| Requests | 150 per model: each case as written, swapped (`--swap`, separate requests) and toned |
| Recordings | `examples/recordings/pairwise-judge-jev-1.13/` and `-jev-1.14/`; `tests/jud_perturb.rs` replays both and fails when a count moves |
| Latency | median 111 ms (1.13) and 122 ms (1.14) a call; 439 input tokens at the median |

## Results

The confident column counts the pairs whose original verdict had a confidence of at least 0.5, 47 of the 50 on both models. Intervals are 95 % Wilson.

| model | test | flip rate | flip rate, confidence ≥ 0.50 | mean \|Δp\| | accuracy, original | accuracy, perturbed |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Jev 1.13 | swap | 0.02 [0.00, 0.10] (1/50) | 0.00 [0.00, 0.08] (0/47) | 0.029 | 0.94 [0.84, 0.98] (47/50) | 0.96 [0.87, 0.99] (48/50) |
| Jev 1.13 | tone | 0.16 [0.08, 0.29] (8/50) | 0.15 [0.07, 0.28] (7/47) | 0.164 | 0.94 [0.84, 0.98] (47/50) | 0.78 [0.65, 0.87] (39/50) |
| Jev 1.14 | swap | 0.02 [0.00, 0.10] (1/50) | 0.00 [0.00, 0.08] (0/47) | 0.031 | 0.94 [0.84, 0.98] (47/50) | 0.96 [0.87, 0.99] (48/50) |
| Jev 1.14 | tone | 0.12 [0.06, 0.24] (6/50) | 0.09 [0.03, 0.20] (4/47) | 0.129 | 0.94 [0.84, 0.98] (47/50) | 0.86 [0.74, 0.93] (43/50) |

- **The swap moved one verdict, an unsure one.** On both models the only flip is `llmbar-natural-042`, a pair whose better answer is `b`, which both picked as `a` at a confidence of 0.36 and 0.32 and as `b` once the order was reversed. No verdict of confidence 0.5 or more moved, and the mean change in probability was three points. The paper's typed models all changed some verdicts under a swap, and these two did, once each; at one flip in fifty, on a verdict a gate would not have acted on, the order is close to irrelevant on these pairs. They are short and most have one clearly better answer, where a judge has little reason to fall back on position, so this says nothing about harder pairs.
- **The tone moved more, and confident verdicts too.** Jev 1.13 flipped 8 of 50, every one a right verdict made wrong, and fell from 0.94 to 0.78; Jev 1.14 flipped 6, five made wrong and one corrected, and fell to 0.86. Seven and four of those flips were verdicts at a confidence of 0.5 or more, so a gate at that bar would have acted on them. The cases that moved: on 1.13, `021`, `038`, `040`, `045`, `067`, `092`, `096` and `099`; on 1.14, `021`, `040`, `045`, `067`, `069` and `092`, of which `069`, a miss as written, became right.
- **No one tone did it.** The 1.13 flips were 3 angry, 2 cheerful, 2 sad and 1 fearful; the 1.14 flips 3 cheerful, 2 angry and 1 sad. Twelve or thirteen cases per tone is too few to rank them.
- **1.14 is less moved by tone than 1.13**, by 4 flips in 50; the intervals overlap, so fifty pairs do not show the difference to be real.

## Agreement between the two versions

Added on 2026-10-24 with `jud eval --against`, from the same recordings, no call:

```sh
jud eval examples/jud/pairwise-judge.jud examples/jud/pairwise-judge-cases.jud \
  --replay examples/recordings/pairwise-judge-jev-1.14 \
  --against examples/recordings/pairwise-judge-jev-1.13
```

| question | pairs | differs | differs, confidence ≥ 0.50 | mean \|Δp\| | accuracy | accuracy, against |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---|---|
| better | 50 | 0.00 [0.00, 0.07] (0/50) | 0.00 [0.00, 0.08] (0/47) | 0.016 | 0.94 [0.84, 0.98] (47/50) | 0.94 [0.84, 0.98] (47/50) |

Jev 1.14 picks what Jev 1.13 picks on every case as written, and its probability on the pick is within two points of 1.13's on average. They agree on their misses too, the same three, which is why agreement is a screen and not a grade ([Agreement before labels](../../concepts/rubrics-cases-recordings.md#agreement-before-labels)). The two versions differ only once the request is perturbed (the tone rows above). `tests/jud_perturb.rs` replays it.

## What this does not show

- **Fifty pairs.** Every rate above carries an interval ten to twenty points wide. A conclusion about a judge on a task needs that task's cases, in the hundreds.
- **The rewrites are this repository's.** They keep each better answer's content, but some add a hedge ("I hope that's right") that a careful judge could fairly hold against an answer. CALM generated its rewrites with GPT-4 Turbo; these were written by hand for the example.
- **The swap is asked in a separate request** (`--swap=separate`) under the id `better.swapped`, so that it is a request of its own to the recordings. TypeSafe documents that the id is not sent to the model ([Position and tone](../../reference/cli.md#position-and-tone)), so on these two models the two requests differ only in order.


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/laya-typed-decisions.md -->


# Against Laya typed-decisions

The [judgment crate](../../../README.md) was written against TypeSafe's documented wire and tested against mocks of it. A mock encodes what the client author believed about the wire; only a real server can contradict that belief. This page records the first such contradiction test: the crate against [Laya](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya)'s `typed-decisions` checkpoint, served by Laya's own HTTP server, on the benchmark the checkpoint was fine-tuned for. The question was narrow: does the crate work, unchanged, against a second implementation of the System One wire, and if not, what has to change on which side.

The short answer: yes, after one fix in the crate that TypeSafe's own API would have needed too. Everything the crate sends is accepted, everything Laya returns decodes through the typed handles, errors are classified as documented (a 401 is `Unauthorized` and is not retried; no run has provoked a status that is retried), and the benchmark replays through the crate's evaluation module to numbers in line with the model card. Four differences between the two servers were found; none needs code, all are recorded below so the next person does not rediscover them. A second run on 2026-10-03, against `laya-serve` 0.3.24, found one more thing that needed code, in the same place as the first: the legend comparison ([below](#re-run-against-laya-serve-0324)).

## What was tested, and with what

| | |
|---|---|
| Model | [convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions), revision `1a793eb` (2026-09-24), Apache 2.0. ModernBERT-large encoder, 421M parameters, fine-tuned on the typed-decisions training split with RLCD |
| Server | `laya-serve` from the `laya` PyPI package, 0.3.20, with `LAYA_MODELS=typed-decisions`; torch 2.14 CPU, transformers 5.17 |
| Weights served | The server loads the checkpoint from the `typed-decisions/` folder of the `convaiinnovations/laya` bundle; its `model.safetensors` has the same SHA-256 as the standalone repository's (`4fa56de7…07a24e`, 842,609,220 bytes), so the two are one model |
| Machine | 4 CPUs, 15 GB, no GPU, in the development container; every latency below is CPU latency |
| Crate | `judgment` at the commit this page was added in, built with its default `http` feature |
| Benchmark | [LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions), `test` split: 400 cases, 5 questions each, across four workflows, with a gold label and distribution per question, Apache 2.0 |

Nothing here touched TypeSafe's hosted API: no key was available in the environment, so the comparison with Jev is against the numbers the benchmark and the model card publish, not a run of our own. That gap is stated where it matters; the same live tests were later run against the hosted API, in [judgment against the hosted TypeSafe API](hosted-typesafe.md).

## Why a test, rather than reading the two specifications

Laya's README says its payload is schema-identical to Jev's and lists three differences. The crate's rustdoc says which of TypeSafe's limits it enforces before sending. Comparing the two documents would have found the option-count difference and missed everything else the run found: the model list endpoint that the README documents and the server does not serve, the object level that neither document says is echoed verbatim, the model name that the router silently redirects. Each of those is a fact about running code, discoverable only by running it. The tests are kept so the next server, or the next Laya release, is checked the same way instead of by re-reading.

## The tests

The live checks are in `tests/live.rs`. Every one is `#[ignore]`, so the gate stays hermetic and they run only by hand:

```sh
JUDGMENT_LIVE_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 JUDGMENT_LIVE_MODEL=typed-decisions JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE=laya \
  cargo test -p judgment --test live -- --ignored --nocapture
```

Each test exists for one belief the mocks could not check.

| Test | Asserts | Why it is there |
|---|---|---|
| `the_three_primitives_round_trip_through_typed_handles` | A Choice over an `options!` enum, a Noul with criteria and a three-level Score come back through their handles: the chosen option is the arg max of a distribution that sums to 1 within rounding, the legend echoes the levels in order, the score lies on the level line, confidence and probability are in `[0, 1]`, the response names a model and counts input tokens. It also prints the request id and the names of the undocumented top-level fields, without asserting either | The whole promise of the crate is that the handle fixes the answer's type. Laya rounds every probability to four decimals and adds fields the API does not have (`answer_confidence`, `action`, `routing`); the test shows the typed views survive both |
| `a_structured_score_level_comes_back_decoded` | A level sent as an object (`{"what": …, "examples": […]}`) decodes, and its label is the object's JSON | This is the test that failed first. See [the bug](#the-bug-the-run-caught) |
| `a_structured_score_level_is_echoed` | An object level, an array level and a string level are sent, the body fetched directly rather than through the client, the legend printed exactly as the server echoed it, and `Response::verify` passes on it | `verify` accepts a structured level echoed as itself or as text that parses to it; the test prints which form a server uses: the value on the hosted API and on `laya-serve` to 0.3.21, Python-spaced text from 0.3.22 ([the re-run](#re-run-against-laya-serve-0324)). Added with judgment 0.2 |
| `a_choice_option_without_a_description_is_accepted` | `dynamic_choice` with `None` descriptions is answered | TypeSafe documents `null` descriptions; Laya's README says every option needs a description. The server accepts them |
| `the_model_list_is_either_served_or_absent` | `list_models` returns a non-empty list or exactly `Error::Http { status: 404 }`; anything else fails | `GET /v1/models` is in TypeSafe's OpenAPI document and both SDKs call it, but the HTTP API reference page leaves it out, and a compatible server may not serve it. The crate must fail cleanly rather than hang or misdecode |
| `a_model_name_the_server_does_not_know_is_still_answered` | A client sending the crate's default `jev-latest` gets an answer | A consumer that only changed `base_url` must not be broken by the model name it never set |
| `a_live_answer_replays_offline_from_its_recording` | `Recorder` over the live client, then `Replay` over the directory, return the same `Response` for the same state and questions | The request hash that keys a recording is computed on the crate side; this proves it is stable across a real round trip, which the mocks could not, since they never see a serialised request |
| `an_unknown_extra_field_is_answered_or_refused_by_name` | A request carrying an unknown `CallOptions::extra` field is either answered or refused as `Error::InvalidRequest` with status 400 or 422, and the test prints which; a 5xx, a transport failure or a decode error fails | The crate sends extra fields as given and leaves the choice to the server, so either outcome is a pass, but only a run says which one a server takes. Added with judgment 0.2 |
| `the_builder_refuses_what_the_reference_page_forbids` | 256 options, one level and a null level are refused by the builder before any request | Listed with the live tests so a run shows the limits next to the behaviour they guard; it needs no server. The limits are the HTTP API reference page's; TypeSafe's OpenAPI document states none above and only one level below, so the builder is the stricter, and what a server does past them is unverified (`tests/contract.rs` pins the difference). Named `the_builder_refuses_what_the_wire_would_reject` when this run was made |
| `a_wrong_bearer_token_is_unauthorized_and_the_right_one_is_not` | Against a second server started with `LAYA_API_KEY`, a wrong key is `Error::Unauthorized` and the right one is answered, and the 401's request id is printed; skipped unless `JUDGMENT_LIVE_AUTH_BASE_URL` is set | The retry loop must not retry a 401 and the error must be the one whose remedy is "check the key". Laya returns FastAPI's `{"detail": …}` body rather than TypeSafe's `{"error": …}`; the classification is by status, so the body shape does not matter |

The eight tests of the first run, all but the two added with judgment 0.2, passed on 2026-09-24 against the two servers described above.

With judgment 0.2.0, all ten passed on 2026-09-25 against the same two servers, `laya-serve` 0.3.20. What that run showed, beyond the assertions:

- Structured levels are echoed verbatim: the object level came back as a JSON object and the array level as a JSON array, never as their compact JSON in a string, so `verify`'s second form has still not been observed.
- The unknown extra field was answered, not refused.
- The top-level `routing` field arrived in `Response::extra`.
- The server sends no `x-typesafe-request-id` header, so the printed request id was `None`. This is an observation from the printed output; no test asserts it.

The benchmark was not re-run live; the committed recordings replay under 0.2 to the same report as before ([below](#what-the-benchmark-measured)).

The benchmark replay is `examples/typed_decisions.rs`. It reads one case per line, builds the crate's `Questions` from each case's wire JSON through the public builders, sends every case through one `dyn SystemOne`, and grades each answer against the gold label with `judgment::eval` (commands run from the crate's directory):

```sh
# live, recording every answer
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 TYPESAFE_MODEL=typed-decisions TYPESAFE_API_KEY=unused \
  cargo run -p judgment --example typed_decisions -- \
    examples/typed-decisions/sample.jsonl --record /tmp/laya-run

# offline, from the recordings: no server, no key, same numbers
cargo run -p judgment --example typed_decisions -- \
  examples/typed-decisions/sample.jsonl --replay /tmp/laya-run
```

`examples/typed-decisions/sample.jsonl` is the first ten test cases of each workflow, committed so the example runs from a checkout; `tools/typed-decisions/export.py` writes the full split from the Parquet files. The example is a compatibility test at scale before it is an evaluation: 400 cases is 2,000 questions through the builder, 400 requests through the client, 2,000 answers through the decoder, and every combination of primitive and criteria shape the benchmark uses (Noul with and without criteria, Choice with three to five described options, Score with three to five levels).

## The bug the run caught

TypeSafe documents that a Score level may be a string or an object, and that the answer's `legend` maps each level number "back to its description". The crate typed the legend as `BTreeMap<String, String>` and the builder accepted any JSON value as a level. Laya, given an object level, echoes the object; the crate then failed to decode the whole response, not just that question, because one legend value was not a string. Reading TypeSafe's wording again, Jev would echo the object too: the legend is the level, not a summary of it.

The fix is in the crate. The legend now holds JSON values, and the typed `Score` view labels a level by its string or, for a structured level, by its compact JSON, so a log line or a note always has text without re-deriving it from the question. The builder also refuses a `null` level before sending: a level is "described in words" and a null has no meaning the API defines, but Laya accepts it and echoes `null` into the legend, which is one more way a response can fail to decode. Two unit tests cover the change without a server; the live test above covers it with one. A consumer whose Score levels are strings sees no change.

## What the two servers do differently

None of these needs a code change; each is a fact to know when pointing the crate at Laya.

- **The model name routes, and the response does not say where.** `laya-serve` maps `model` onto a checkpoint by name: `typed-decisions` or the full repository id picks the fine-tuned one, and any other value, including the crate's default `jev-latest`, lets Laya's router choose by language, which for English text means the base checkpoint, loaded on demand. With `LAYA_MODELS=typed-decisions` preloaded, a request that named no model still took 78 s the first time while the base checkpoint downloaded. The response's `model` field is `laya-rl-agent` for every checkpoint; which one answered is in a top-level `routing` object. The crate ignored it when this run was made; since judgment 0.2 it is kept, as it came, in `Response::extra`, the map of every top-level field the API does not document, so a caller can log it without a second decoder. Consequence: set `.model("typed-decisions")` on the builder, and do not rely on `Response::model` to tell checkpoints apart; read `Response::extra["routing"]` when the checkpoint matters.
- **No `GET /v1/models`.** `laya-serve` has never served it: 0.3.20 has `/health` and `POST /v1/systemone`, 0.3.22 added `POST /v1/systemone/batch`, and the `GET /models` in Laya's README belongs to its example server, not to `laya-serve`. `list_models` returns `Error::Http { status: 404 }`. A consumer that lists models has nothing to list; the shim under `tools/systemone/` still serves it.
- **Latency is seconds, and the default timeout is ten.** A five-question case takes about two seconds on four CPU cores, warm. The crate's default per-attempt timeout mirrors the hosted API's hundreds of milliseconds; the example and the live tests set 120 s, and a consumer pointing at Laya sets its own.
- **Confidence means something else.** TypeSafe computes `confidence` from the spread of the distribution; Laya reports one minus the normalised entropy under that name and adds `answer_confidence`, the probability of the reported answer, which its model card says to gate on. Both are in `[0, 1]`, so the typed `Confidence` accepts either, but a threshold tuned on Jev's confidence does not carry over. The answer-level extras, `answer_confidence` and the `action` object, are still ignored: `Response::extra` keeps top-level fields only, and fields inside an answer that the crate does not model are dropped, as the Python SDK drops them. A caller that wants to gate on `answer_confidence` recomputes it from the answer's own `probabilities`. The server also warned at start-up that the checkpoint's temperature for Choice questions with eleven or more options is outside the range it trusts and was clamped; confidence on such questions is uncalibrated by Laya's own account.

Limits were probed as well. Laya 0.3.20 answered 200 options and 11 levels, past its README's stated budget; the crate's builder stops at TypeSafe's 255 and 10 regardless, so the stricter of the two bounds applies. Since 0.3.21 the server refuses more than 100 options on one question with a 413 ([the re-run](#re-run-against-laya-serve-0324)), so on options the server is now the stricter. A malformed body is a 400 with a FastAPI `detail`. The run reported it as `Error::Http` with the body; the crate now reports it as `Error::InvalidRequest { status: 400, .. }`, the same variant as TypeSafe's 422, with the message read from `detail` (or `error`, which the shim under `tools/systemone/` sends), and still not retried.

## What the benchmark measured

The full `test` split, 400 cases and 2,000 questions, through the crate against the server above, on 2026-09-24. Accuracy is the share of questions whose reported answer is the gold label. Calibration is graded on the probability of the reported answer (for a Noul, `max(p, 1 − p)`), not on the wire's `confidence` field, because that field is a different quantity on each server ([above](#what-the-two-servers-do-differently)) and the model card's own ECE is on the answer's probability. Brier is the crate's multi-class form, the squared distance between the reported distribution and the one-hot label summed over options, which is not the model card's definition and is not compared with it.

| Slice | n | Accuracy | Model card | ECE | Brier (crate) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All questions | 2,000 | 0.766 | 0.766 | 0.213 | 0.400 |
| Noul | 600 | 0.857 | 0.857 | 0.192 | 0.287 |
| Choice | 600 | 0.733 | 0.733 | 0.255 | 0.465 |
| Score | 800 | 0.723 | 0.723 | 0.198 | 0.435 |
| agent_trace_observability | 500 | 0.730 | 0.730 | 0.229 | 0.461 |
| customer_service | 500 | 0.764 | 0.764 | 0.210 | 0.396 |
| invoice_processing | 500 | 0.804 | 0.804 | 0.165 | 0.302 |
| security_incidents | 500 | 0.766 | 0.766 | 0.249 | 0.439 |

Every accuracy, overall, per primitive and per workflow, is the model card's figure to the third decimal, and the overall ECE (0.213) is the card's too. That is the compatibility result in one line: the crate's builders, client, decoder and grading reproduce the publisher's own evaluation of the model, so nothing between the case file and the number is lost or misread on the crate side. The card's Brier (0.062) is not reproduced because it is not the same statistic; the crate's is documented on `judgment::eval::metrics::brier`.

The numbers also say what the card says about the model. Mean answer probability was 0.58 when the answer was right and 0.46 when it was wrong, a usable gap, but an ECE of 0.2 means a reported 0.8 was right about 60% of the time: over-confident, as the card states. Noul is the strong primitive, Choice the weak one, and `invoice_processing` the easy workflow.

Latency, per five-question case on four CPU cores, warm, with nothing else running: p50 2.1 s, p95 2.2 s. During the full run, which shared the cores with the build gate and a second server, it was p50 4.1 s and p95 6.2 s; the run is I/O-free, so the difference is CPU contention. The card's tens of milliseconds are on a T4.

The 40-case sample committed with the example was recorded from the same server into `examples/recordings/typed_decisions/`; replaying it offline produces the identical report (accuracy 0.725 on 200 questions, the same to every digit as the live run that wrote it), which is the recording round trip checked at benchmark scale rather than on one request. The recordings hold none of Laya's extras (no `routing`, no `action`): the `Recorder` writes the decoded `Response`, and the crate that recorded them dropped what it did not model. A test (`the_committed_recordings_decode_and_rewrite_byte_for_byte` in `tests/backend.rs`) checks that all 40 still decode, with no unknown answer and nothing in `Response::extra`, and write back byte for byte.

## What this does and does not establish

It establishes that the crate is not TypeSafe-specific in any way that matters: a second, independently written server was driven through the public API with one fix, and that fix corrected a reading of TypeSafe's own documentation. It establishes that the evaluation module and the recording backends work against real answers, not only the `Fake`. And it gives a number for the fine-tuned checkpoint on its own benchmark, through this crate, that the model card's number can be compared with.

It does not establish anything about a domain of your own. The checkpoint is fine-tuned for four workflows, and the one out-of-domain probe in the live test, a customer's message about failing payouts, was routed to `technical` with 0.45 probability, which is the model card's warning made concrete. The path to self-hosting on another domain is labelled history replayed through both models with `judgment::eval`, per-question numbers. What this page adds is that the crate side of that path is proven; the remaining work is data.

## Re-run against laya-serve 0.3.24

On 2026-10-03 the live tests were run again, against `laya-serve` 0.3.24 (`laya` 0.3.24 on PyPI, released 2026-10-02; source at [NandhaKishorM/laya](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya), commit `fa9a2a7`), on the same checkpoint and the same kind of machine (4 CPUs, 15 GB, no GPU; torch 2.14 CPU, transformers 5.18). The question a new release of a compatible server raises is whether the wire moved and whether the crate still fits it. The checkpoint had not moved: `/health` names the bundle revision it serves, `55cf4c4e`, published on 2026-09-24, and `typed-decisions/model.safetensors` is the same 842,609,220 bytes; none of the three checkpoints has been republished since. "The latest Laya models" are therefore the models the first run used, and what changed is the server and the package around them.

### What changed on the wire between 0.3.20 and 0.3.24

Read from the five source distributions (each change is dated by the first release whose `laya/serve.py` or `laya/agent.py` carries it) and confirmed by running the tests.

| Change | Since | What it meant for the crate |
|---|---|---|
| A structured Score level, an object or an array, is echoed in the legend as JSON text: `render_criterion` in `laya/common.py` (`json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(", ", ": "), default=str)`), which already rendered what the model was shown, is applied to the legend from 0.3.22 on; 0.3.20 and 0.3.21 echoed the value | 0.3.22 | `Response::verify` compared a text echo with the crate's compact JSON and refused every structured level; the two structured-level tests failed. Fixed in the crate ([below](#the-second-fix)) |
| Limits checked before inference and answered 413 with a `detail` sentence: more than 64 questions, a state over 50,000 characters and a body over 2 MiB in 0.3.20 already (the first run sent none of those); more than 100 options or 32 levels on one question, and more than 512 options in all, from 0.3.21 (0.3.20 answered 200 options and 11 levels) | 0.3.20 | A 413 was `Error::Http`, a status with no remedy attached. It is now `Error::InvalidRequest { status: 413, .. }`, not retried, and `Error::is_request_too_large`, the predicate that also names the hosted API's 400 `max_tokens_exceeded` |
| A `null` Score level is a 422 (`score question … has a null level at index …`); 0.3.20 accepted it and echoed `null` | 0.3.24 | None: the builder has refused a null level since the first run, for this reason |
| `POST /v1/systemone/batch`, many states under one set of questions, at most 64 | 0.3.22 | None: the crate sends one request per state by design, and one request already carries many questions |
| `LAYA_JEV_STRICT=1` serves the documented shape only: no `routing`, no `answer_confidence` or `action`, a Noul answer with `noul` alone, `usage` with the two counts | 0.3.24 | None either way: the crate reads both shapes. With it `Response::extra` is empty; without, it holds `routing` |
| `Server-Timing: inference;dur=<ms>` and `X-Inference-Time-Ms` on every answer; past `LAYA_MAX_CONCURRENT` (16) requests, a 503 `server busy, try again later` with `Retry-After: 1` | 0.3.21 | None: the headers are not read (the `typesafe.evaluate` span times the call), and the retry loop already honours a `Retry-After` on any 5xx it retries |
| Request fields read as inference controls: `max_len` and `head_max_len` (0.3.21), then `task`, `lang`, `lang_guess` and `min_confidence` (0.3.22), beside `model`; a bad value is a 422 naming the field | 0.3.21 | `CallOptions::extra` carries them. The hosted API refuses every extra top-level field with a 400, so a caller sets them for Laya only. `min_confidence` adds `low_confidence`, `abstention` and `abstention_threshold` inside each answer, which the crate drops with the other answer-level extras; gate on `probabilities` instead |

Unchanged, and still as the first run recorded: no `GET /v1/models`; `model` is `laya-rl-agent` whatever checkpoint answered, with the checkpoint in `routing`; an unknown model name is routed, not refused; `confidence` is one minus the normalised entropy, not TypeSafe's spread; FastAPI's `{"detail": …}` error bodies; no request id header. New in the full payload since the first run, and ignored by the crate like the Noul `confidence` (`max(p, 1 − p)`) that was already there: four more `usage` keys (`state_tokens`, `state_tokens_dropped`, `truncated`, `truncated_questions`).

### The second fix

The crate's rule was that a structured level is echoed as itself or as its compact JSON, compared as text. The second form had never been seen, the first was what both servers did, and the hosted API still does it ([hosted record](hosted-typesafe.md#what-the-hosted-api-does)). `laya-serve` 0.3.22 echoes the text it rendered for the model: `{"what": "cosmetic", "examples": ["a typo in the invoice footer"]}` came back as the string `{"examples": ["a typo in the invoice footer"], "what": "cosmetic"}`, the keys in the order the crate sent them (serde's sorted order) and Python's `", "` and `": "` between them, which is neither the value nor the compact `{"examples":["a typo in the invoice footer"],"what":"cosmetic"}`. `verify` refused it as `legend level 0 is not the level the question sent`, and with it the whole response, which is exactly what it is for when a legend is not the levels sent; here the legend was the levels sent, written differently.

The fix compares a structured level by what the echo parses to: the same JSON value, or a string that parses to that value, whatever its spacing or key order. A string level is still matched by text alone and never parsed, and a number written differently (`1.0` for `1`) is still a different value. `Score::levels` labels a structured level with its compact JSON whichever way it was echoed, so a label reads the same from both servers and carries none of a server's spacing; the one string level a label does not keep verbatim is one whose own text is a JSON object or array, which is re-spaced the same way. Unit tests pin the three forms and the refusals; the live test `a_structured_score_level_is_echoed` keeps printing the echo, so a fourth form shows up in a run before it fails a caller. A consumer whose levels are strings sees no change.

### What the run showed

All fifteen tests pass against three servers on `laya` 0.3.24: `laya-serve` with its full payload; `laya-serve` with `LAYA_JEV_STRICT=1` and `LAYA_API_KEY` set, which runs the bearer test too; and the shim at `tools/systemone/serve.py` (its `laya` backend), which answers `GET /v1/models` and has no limits of its own (256 options are a 400 from Laya itself, `only 255 of its 256 option markers fit in max_len=1024`, and the 50,000-character state is answered after truncation). The suite takes about nine seconds on four cores.

- **Limits.** 256 options are a 413, `too many choice options for 'c' (256 > 100)`; 11 levels are answered; one option and one level are answered with probability 1, as on the hosted API.
- **The over-budget state.** 413 `state too large (50600 > 50000 chars)`, which `is_request_too_large` names; the hosted API's 400 `max_tokens_exceeded` is the other side of the same predicate.
- **Stability.** Three identical requests: a spread of 0.000 on every probability and on the score. CPU inference is deterministic where the hosted API moved by up to 0.05 on the same request ([hosted record](hosted-typesafe.md)).
- **Confidence.** The wire's 0.05 against 0.172 from TypeSafe's Choice formula, 0.42 against 0.589 from the Score formula: Laya's quantity is a different one ([above](#what-the-two-servers-do-differently)), and the gap is now a number `Choice::confidence_from_probabilities` gives a caller. `Score::expected_value`, 1.726, agrees with the wire's score, 1.73.
- **The rest.** An empty question id is a 422 where the hosted API's is a 400; the unknown extra field is answered; `jev-latest` is answered by the router, which loaded the English checkpoint on demand to do it; `Response::extra` holds `routing` on the full payload and nothing in strict mode; no response carried a request id.
- **The benchmark sample.** `examples/typed-decisions/sample.jsonl`, 40 cases and 200 questions, recorded live: accuracy 0.725, Brier 0.419, ECE 0.183, the committed recordings' figures to every digit, and the replay of the new recordings gives them again. Answer by answer, the 40 new recordings equal the committed ones but for the `routing` block the crate now keeps in `extra` and the elapsed time: same weights, same prompt for string criteria, same answers. Latency per five-question case was p50 4.6 s and p95 5.8 s, with the build gate and two other servers sharing the cores.
- **The pattern examples.** `fan_out`, `confidence_routing`, `composite_scoring` and `intent_routing` run end to end with `--live` against the server. Their decisions are not Jev's recorded ones, and are not meant to be: the fine-tuned checkpoint puts intent confidence under 0.1 on most of the intent-routing messages, so that pattern's floor sends every message to a person, which is the pattern doing its job on a model that is unsure out of its domain. Here they are a round trip at the application's level, not a measurement.

What this adds to the first run's conclusion: a compatible server can change what it echoes between patch releases without changing its contract, and the crate's response check is where that surfaces, as a refused response rather than a wrong answer. The crate now reads what both servers write; the live tests, re-run against each release, are how the next change is found.

## Repeating the run

From the crate's directory:

```sh
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
.venv/bin/pip install "laya[serve]==0.3.24" pyarrow huggingface_hub   # the release this page last verified

# the server, typed-decisions only, on CPU
USE_TF=0 LAYA_MODELS=typed-decisions LAYA_DEVICE=cpu LAYA_THREADS=4 LAYA_PORT=8000 .venv/bin/laya-serve
# a second one that checks keys and serves the strict Jev shape, for the bearer test and the other shape
USE_TF=0 LAYA_MODELS=typed-decisions LAYA_DEVICE=cpu LAYA_PORT=8001 LAYA_API_KEY=secret LAYA_JEV_STRICT=1 .venv/bin/laya-serve
# the shim, the one server with GET /v1/models (from the crate directory)
USE_TF=0 .venv/bin/python tools/systemone/serve.py laya --models typed-decisions --port 8099

# the live tests
JUDGMENT_LIVE_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 JUDGMENT_LIVE_MODEL=typed-decisions JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE=laya \
JUDGMENT_LIVE_AUTH_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8001 JUDGMENT_LIVE_AUTH_API_KEY=secret \
  cargo test -p judgment --test live -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1

# the full benchmark
.venv/bin/python tools/typed-decisions/export.py --split test --out /tmp/typed-decisions-test.jsonl
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 TYPESAFE_MODEL=typed-decisions TYPESAFE_API_KEY=unused \
  cargo run -p judgment --example typed_decisions -- /tmp/typed-decisions-test.jsonl --record /tmp/laya-full --json
```

`--test-threads=1` keeps the tests from queueing behind each other on a single-worker server. Expect the first request to a checkpoint to include its load time, and the benchmark to take about a quarter of an hour on four cores. The test that sends `jev-latest` makes the router load the English checkpoint beside the fine-tuned one (843 MB more), so the server needs memory for both. Point `JUDGMENT_LIVE_BASE_URL` at port 8099, with `JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE=generic`, to run the suite against the shim: it refuses 256 options with a 400 and answers the over-budget state after truncating it, where the `laya` profile pins laya-serve's 413s.


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/autojev-serve.md -->


# Against autojev-serve

Perplexity's [pplx-decider-v1.1-27b](https://huggingface.co/perplexity-ai/pplx-decider-v1.1-27b) is a decision model, a classifier with a 255-row decision head, not a chat model. Its checkpoint ships its own HTTP server, `autojev-serve`, which serves `POST /v1/systemone` and `GET /v1/models`. `mise run live:pplx` runs the live tests against it with `JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE=autojev`; this page is what that profile pins and where each pin comes from.

The short answer: the wire holds. Every body the server sent conforms to the vendored OpenAPI document, refusals included. Where it differs from the hosted API is where the document is silent: which requests it refuses, and with which status.

## What was tested, and with what

| | |
|---|---|
| Server | `autojev/server.py` from the checkpoint's `source/` (the FastAPI app reports version 0.2.0), run unchanged |
| Model | Not the real one: it needs a CUDA GPU with about 49 GiB for its weights, and the run had none. `answer()`, `options()` and `describe()` from the checkpoint's `model.py` ran unchanged; only the network was replaced, by deterministic logits hashed from each row |
| Machine | 4 CPUs, 15 GB, no GPU, in the development container |
| Date | 2026-10-09 |
| Profiles | `autojev` and `generic`, model `autojev-qwen3.8-27b`; `autojev` again with the model named `jev-latest` |

Everything the server decides before the model runs is the real server's: request validation, the status of each refusal, the body shapes, the aliases, the model list, the bearer check. What depends on the model is not shown here: accuracy, calibration, the confidence formulas, and what the real tokenizer does past its window.

## What the server does

| Request | autojev-serve | The hosted API |
|---|---|---|
| The three primitives, a structured level, an option with no description | 200, conforming to `SystemOneResponse` | 200 |
| 256 options | 422, `HTTPValidationError` (`Dictionary should have at most 255 items`) | 400, `at most 255` |
| 11 levels | 422, `HTTPValidationError` (`List should have at most 10 items`) | 400 |
| One option | 200, probability 1 | 200, probability 1 |
| One level | 422, `HTTPValidationError` (`List should have at least 2 items`) | 200 |
| An empty question id | 200, answered under the key `""` | 400, `cannot be empty` |
| A state of about 40,000 tokens | answered: no budget is checked before the model | 400, `max_tokens_exceeded` |
| An unknown extra body field | 422, `Extra inputs are not permitted` | 400, `Invalid request.` |
| `GET /v1/models` | 200, conforming to `ModelMetadataList`: `autojev`, `autojev-qwen3.8-27b`, `jev-1.13.0`, `jev-latest`, `jev-preview` | 200 |
| A wrong bearer token, with `AUTOJEV_API_KEY` set | 401 | 401 |

Two things the hosted API sends and this server does not are both allowed by the document: a Noul answer with no `confidence` (`NoulAnswer` requires only `noul` and `type`) and `output_tokens` always 0.

## Why the profile, and not the model name

The server answers to `jev-latest`, `jev-preview` and `jev-1.13.0` as well as its own names. The live tests used to take any model whose name starts with `jev` for the hosted API and assert its status codes, so a run under an alias failed on 422 against 400. The tests now take the server from `JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE` ([How the crate is checked](method.md)), and the same run passes under `jev-latest`. Name the model `autojev-qwen3.8-27b` anyway, so a recording or a report does not say Jev.

## What is still open

A run on a GPU with the real weights: the decisions themselves, the confidence the model gives, and the over-budget state, which the real tokenizer may truncate or refuse. That run belongs on this page, with the checkpoint's revision.

## How to repeat it

```sh
# on a CUDA host, with the snapshot's source/ installed with its requirements.txt
AUTOJEV_CHECKPOINT=<snapshot> PORT=8010 autojev-serve

# from the crate's root: the live tests under the autojev profile
PPLX_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8010 mise run live:pplx
```


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/liquid.md -->


# Against Liquid's System One API

Liquid serves TypeSafe's System One API for its decision models `d1` and `d1-ultra` at `https://api.liquid.ai/decisions`: the client reaches `POST /decisions/v1/systemone` and `GET /decisions/v1/models` with that as its base URL and no other change. `mise run live:liquid` runs the live tests against it with `JUDGMENT_LIVE_PROFILE=liquid`; this page is what that profile pins and where each pin comes from.

The short answer: the wire holds, for text and, sent as Liquid spells them, for images. Every success body conforms to the vendored OpenAPI document, and the confidence formulas hold within rounding. Liquid differs from the hosted API in its refusals: it refuses with 422 where the hosted API answers 400 or 200, in OpenAI's error envelope rather than the document's `HTTPValidationError`; it refuses a model name it does not serve; and it has no Box question.

## What was tested, and with what

| | |
|---|---|
| Server | `https://api.liquid.ai/decisions`, Liquid's hosted API |
| Model | `d1`, then `d1-ultra` |
| Reference | Liquid's API reference ("Liquid inference API" 1.0.0), the decision models' section, read from the Liquid console (`https://console.liquid.ai/docs`, behind a sign-in) |
| Date | 2026-10-18 |
| Profiles | `generic` first on `d1`, then `liquid` on both models; all 19 tests pass under `liquid` on each, the shared-images test (`JUDGMENT_LIVE_SHARED_IMAGES=1`) included |

## What the server does

| Request | Liquid, `d1` | The hosted API |
|---|---|---|
| The three primitives, a structured level, an option with no description | 200, conforming to `SystemOneResponse`; a first request by hand also carried `usage.cost` in US dollars, which `Usage::cost` reads | 200 |
| 256 options | 422, `A Choice accepts at most 255 options.` | 400, `at most 255` |
| 11 levels | 422, `A Score accepts at most 10 levels.` | 400 |
| One option | 422, `A Choice needs at least 2 options.` | 200, probability 1 |
| One level | 422, `A Score needs at least 2 levels.` | 200 |
| An empty question id | 422, `Invalid key in record` | 400, `cannot be empty` |
| A state of about 40,000 tokens in about 500 KB of text, with or without long context asked for | 422, `over the model's input limit of 65536 tokens, images included, or 250000 bytes of text`: the bytes, not the tokens | 400, `max_tokens_exceeded`; answered under long context |
| An unknown extra body field | answered, the field ignored | 400, `Invalid request.` |
| The model name `jev-latest` | 404, `not_found_error`, `The model `jev-latest` does not exist.` | 200 |
| An image with a Box question | 422, `Invalid discriminator value. Expected 'noul' \| 'choice' \| 'score'` | 200 on `jev-preview` |
| An image as a shared `images` array of bare base64 (`CallOptions::shared_images`) | 422, `An image must be a base64 `data:` URL or a `{ content_type, base64 }` object.` | not served |
| The same array of `data:` URLs (`CallOptions::shared_images_as_data_urls`) | 200 on both models: `circle_present` 1.00 for the drawn circle, against about 0.5 for the same question with no image | not served |
| `GET /v1/models` | 200, conforming to `ModelMetadataList`: `d1`, `d1-ultra` | 200 |
| A wrong bearer token | 401 | 401 |

Refusals come in OpenAI's envelope, `{"error": {"message", "type", "param", "code"}}`, with `type` `invalid_request_error` or `not_found_error` and `code` null. The client keeps `type` as `kind`, and the message as the detail. This is not the document's `HTTPValidationError` for a 422, a `detail` list of located issues: `Error::InvalidRequest::issues` is always empty on Liquid, and the schema check's "conforms" on a refusal means nothing here, since every field of `HTTPValidationError` is optional. The profile checks each refusal's message instead. There is no request id header.

## What the profile pins, and why

- **422 for every refusal** the limits probes, the empty id and the over-budget state draw. Liquid's reference says validation errors return 422, and the run agrees.
- **A model name it does not serve is a 404**, an `Error::Http`, where the hosted API, Laya and autojev-serve answered it (Ollama 0.40.5 also answers 404). A client built for the hosted API, sending `jev-latest`, fails against Liquid until it names `d1`.
- **An over-budget state is not recognisable as one.** `Error::is_request_too_large` reads a 413 or a code that names the budget (`max_tokens_exceeded`, Ollaya's `INPUT_TOO_LONG` and `STATE_TRUNCATED`), and Liquid sends neither: only the message says the state is over the limit. The over-budget test asserts the 422 on Liquid and leaves the predicate out; a caller that needs to tell this refusal from others has only the message to go on. The crate does not read the message, because the wording is Liquid's to change without notice and a predicate that silently stops matching is worse than one that never did.
- **Success bodies hold to the document**, so the profile asserts it, as `typesafe` and `autojev` do.
- **The confidence formulas hold** within the hosted API's tolerances (over three runs on `d1`, the wire's choice confidence 0.84 to 0.85 against 0.844 to 0.846 from the formula, score confidence 0.55 to 0.57 against 0.547 to 0.570, and the score 1.70 to 1.71 against an expected level of 1.698 to 1.713), so the profile asserts them, as `typesafe` does.

Repeated identical requests agree on the answer but not on the hundredths (each run makes three calls; on `d1` the spread was 0.020 to 0.036 in probability and 0 to 0.039 in score over four runs, on `d1-ultra` 0.017 and 0.022), as on the hosted API.

## `d1-ultra`

`d1-ultra` behaved as `d1` did on every row above, with its own limit in the over-budget message (`32768 tokens`) and its own numbers in the confidence check (choice 0.82 against 0.824, score 0.92 against 0.919, score 1.95 against 1.946). One profile covers both.

## What Liquid's reference adds

The decision models' section documents what the runs did not exercise, and the image rules the shared-images rows above follow:

- An `images` array of up to 8 images, each a `data:` URL or a `{ content_type, base64 }` object, on models whose `input_modalities` include `image`; `GET /v1/models` lists `text` and `image` for both `d1` and `d1-ultra` on 2026-10-18. It is Liquid's extension. Ollama's array takes only bare base64 ([what Ollama does differently](../../guides/configure-a-backend.md#what-ollama-does-differently)), so no one spelling serves both, and the crate sends Liquid's with `shared_images_as_data_urls` (judgment-05p).
- Images may also ride in an array state as OpenAI `image_url` parts.
- Up to 128 questions per request; `d1-ultra` allows 32,768 tokens; both allow 250 KB of text.
- 429 with `Retry-After` when the organisation's per-model limit is spent, and with code `model_unavailable` when the model has no healthy target. The client retries a 429 and honours `Retry-After`; neither was observed.

## What is still open

The runs show the wire, not the models: accuracy and calibration on real cases are not measured here. Images were answered for one drawn circle on each model, not measured on cases. A 429 was not drawn.

## How to repeat it

```sh
# LIQUID_API_KEY in .env; spends a handful of model calls on the Liquid account
mise run live:liquid

# the shared-images test as well
JUDGMENT_LIVE_SHARED_IMAGES=1 mise run live:liquid

# another model
LIQUID_MODEL=d1-ultra mise run live:liquid
```


<!-- source: docs/project/verification/ollaya.md -->


# Against Ollaya

[Ollaya](https://ollaya.dev) serves open decision models on your own machine behind an API it documents as wire-identical to TypeSafe's ([TypeSafe compatibility](https://ollaya.dev/docs/typesafe-compatibility)): `POST /v1/systemone`, its alias `POST /v1/decisions`, and `GET /v1/models`, on `http://127.0.0.1:11435` by default. `mise run live:ollaya` runs the live tests against it, under the `ollaya` profile.

The short answer: the wire holds for text, with a real run behind it. Every success body, the model list and every 422's `detail` conform to the vendored OpenAPI document; the 404 and the 401 are statuses the document does not list. The confidence formulas hold, and repeated requests give the same numbers to the last digit. Ollaya departs from the hosted API in three ways a caller must know: every validation refusal is a 422 and a model it has not pulled a 404; each model's context bounds the options and the state far below TypeSafe's; and its `/v1` API, modelled on typesafe-sdk 0.7.1, has no image field and no Box, so a Box is refused and an image is dropped without a word.

## What was tested, and with what

| | |
|---|---|
| Server | Ollaya 0.17.0 (`linux-amd64`), installed with its script pinned to the version (`OLLAYA_VERSION=0.17.0`, `OLLAYA_NO_SERVICE=1`) and started with `ollaya serve` |
| Model | `laya:en` (ModernBERT-large, released 2026-09-23), an 814 MiB store. Ollaya recommends `laya`, a router, on a machine without an NVIDIA GPU; it sends English to `laya:en`, which the run names directly |
| Machine | a Claude Code cloud container: 4 vCPUs, 15 GiB, no GPU, Ubuntu 24.04 (glibc 2.39; Ollaya needs 2.38). The archive is `.tar.zst`, so `zstd` had to be installed first |
| Reference | Ollaya's [API reference](https://ollaya.dev/docs/api) and [TypeSafe compatibility](https://ollaya.dev/docs/typesafe-compatibility) pages, read on 2026-10-25 |
| Date | 2026-10-25 |
| Tests | `tests/live.rs` as `mise run live:ollaya` builds it: 21 tests, the two new ones included (the `multipart` feature adds a twenty-second). Under `generic`, run first with `--all-features` and before the two new tests existed, 18 of 20 passed, the multipart test among them: `a_model_name_the_server_does_not_know_is_still_answered` failed on the 404 and `a_state_over_the_budget_is_refused_as_too_large` on `is_request_too_large`, both pinned below. Under `ollaya`, 21 of 21, and again 21 of 21 against a second instance on `127.0.0.1:11436` started with `OLLAYA_API_KEY`, which runs the bearer test. The shared-images test skipped itself (`JUDGMENT_LIVE_SHARED_IMAGES` unset) |
| Probes | the rows marked *probe* below were sent by hand with `curl` (one is under [How to repeat it](#how-to-repeat-it)); the others come from the tests |
| Latency | a request with a Choice, a Noul and a Score took 0.65 to 0.71 s warm, median 0.68 s. The first request loads the model: 21.5 s on this machine (below) |

## What the server does

| Request | Ollaya, `laya:en` | The hosted API |
|---|---|---|
| The three primitives, a structured level, an option with no description | 200, conforming to `SystemOneResponse` | 200 |
| An unknown top-level field | 200, the field ignored | 400, `Invalid request.` |
| The same body to `/v1/decisions` (*probe*) | 200 | not in the OpenAPI document |
| `GET /v1/models` | 200, TypeSafe's `ModelMetadataList` of the models pulled to the machine (`laya:en`) | 200, the aliases |
| A model it has not pulled (`jev-latest`) | 404, `{"error": "model \"jev-latest:latest\" not found, try pulling it first", "code": "MODEL_NOT_FOUND"}` | 200 |
| 256 options, 11 levels | 422, `INVALID_REQUEST` with TypeSafe's `detail` (`at most 255`, `at most 10`) | 422 from its schema |
| 1 option, 1 level | 422, `INVALID_REQUEST` (`at least 2`) | 200, probability 1 |
| An empty question id | 200, answered | 400 |
| 125 options (*probe*) | 200 | 200 |
| 126 options (*probe*) | 422, `STATE_TRUNCATED`: the options leave the state no room | 200 |
| 130 options (*probe*), 200 options | 422, `TOO_MANY_OPTIONS`, `130 options do not fit the option budget of laya:en` | 200 by the reference's limits; not run |
| A state of 150 words, 330 input tokens (*probe*) | 200 | 200 |
| A state of 300 to 2,000 words (300 to 450 by *probe*) | 422, `STATE_TRUNCATED`, `part of state was dropped to fit the context of laya:en` | 200 by the reference's limits; not run |
| A state of 162,923 tokens | 422, `INPUT_TOO_LONG`, issue `input_too_long`, `the limit is 65536` | 400, `max_tokens_exceeded` |
| A Box question | 422, `INVALID_REQUEST`, naming the `box` tag against the tags it knows, `choice`, `score`, `noul` | 200 on Jev 1.14 |
| A Noul about an image in `assets`, with the images header | 200, the same answer and the same 42 input tokens as without the image | 200, the image read |
| The same image in Ollama's shared `images` array (*probe*) | 200, the same answer and tokens | not in the OpenAPI document |
| A wrong bearer, no `OLLAYA_API_KEY` set (*probe*) | 200: no key is checked | 401 |
| A wrong bearer, `OLLAYA_API_KEY` set | 401, `UNAUTHORIZED` | 401 |
| Three identical requests | the same probabilities, confidences and score to the fourth decimal | 0.01 to 0.19 apart, wider on ambiguous cases |
| The first request after the model is unloaded, with a 10 s limit (*probe*) | no answer within 10 s; the load carries on, and the next request was answered 9.2 s later | not applicable |

Refusals carry Ollaya's own envelope, `{"error", "code", "detail"}`: a string message, a machine-readable code, and, for `INVALID_REQUEST`, `TOO_MANY_OPTIONS`, `INPUT_TOO_LONG` and `STATE_TRUNCATED`, TypeSafe's `detail` list of located issues. The client reads `error` as the message and `detail` as it does the hosted API's, so `Error::InvalidRequest::issues` holds the issues and each one's `kind` (`too_long`, `state_truncated`, `input_too_long`); the top-level `code` is `kind` (`STATE_TRUNCATED`). A 404 is an `Error::Http`. Every response carries `x-typesafe-request-id`.

The cold load is longer than the crate's default timeout of 10 s. The first attempt times out, and the client's default transport policy retries it; Ollaya keeps loading through the dropped request, as its compatibility page says, so the retry finds the model warm or nearly so. On this machine the retry was answered at 9.2 s, under the limit with little to spare: on a slower one, or a larger model, raise the timeout for the first call or load the model first (`ollaya run`, or Ollaya's `/api/decide` with `keep_alive`). The live suite builds its client with 120 s, so the run did not draw this.

## What the profile pins, and why

- **422 for every limits probe**, and the message naming the bound, as on Liquid.
- **A model it has not pulled is a 404 with `MODEL_NOT_FOUND`**, where the hosted API answers `jev-latest`. A client built for the hosted API fails against Ollaya until it names an Ollaya model; Ollaya's own page says to set `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL`.
- **An empty question id is answered**, as autojev-serve does.
- **An over-budget state is a 422 `INPUT_TOO_LONG`, with the issue `input_too_long`**, which `Error::is_request_too_large` reads as too large, as it does `STATE_TRUNCATED`; `TOO_MANY_OPTIONS` it does not, since the fix is fewer options. `STATE_TRUNCATED` also comes from options that leave the state no room (126 on `laya:en`), where fewer options, not less state, is the fix. Ollaya's limit does not move with the long-context header (the live test's long-context request was refused the same way), so a caller that asks for long context on that predicate is refused again and has to send less.
- **Each model's context bounds the options and the state** (`the_model_s_context_bounds_the_options_and_the_state`). On `laya:en`, whose figures were measured, 200 options are `TOO_MANY_OPTIONS` and a 2,000-word state is `STATE_TRUNCATED`, both 422, and both are pinned. Another model may answer either, or refuse the 200 options as `STATE_TRUNCATED` for the room they leave the state, so for it the test asserts only that a refusal is one of the two. The documented figures for `laya:en`, a 512-token context and about 125 options, held: 125 options were answered and 126 were not. A caller must cap options and shorten states per model, far below TypeSafe's 255 options and 65,536 tokens: Ollaya's `/v1` refuses rather than answer from part of the state.
- **A Box is refused**, a 422 naming the `box` tag and the tags Ollaya knows.
- **An image is dropped without a word** (`an_image_the_model_cannot_see_is_answered_without_it`): the answer and the input tokens are those of the request without it. Ollaya's API page says why: `/v1/systemone` stays identical to TypeSafe's API, which has no image field there, and unknown fields are ignored. Its vision models (`decider:2b-vision`, `winnow:e4b-vision` and others) read images only on its native `/api/decide`, which the crate does not speak. So a rubric about an image must not be pointed at Ollaya's `/v1` at all, whatever the model; the test fails the day a release starts reading them, and the profile is revisited then.
- **Success bodies hold to the document**, so the profile asserts it, as `typesafe`, `autojev` and `liquid` do.
- **The confidence formulas hold** (choice 0.64 on the wire against 0.639 from the formula, score confidence 0.93 against 0.926, score 1.95 against an expected level of 1.951), so the profile asserts them; Ollaya's reference documents TypeSafe's formula.

## What Ollaya's reference adds

The [API reference](https://ollaya.dev/docs/api) documents what the run did not exercise:

- 1 to 256 questions per request; a body over 8 MiB is a 413 `REQUEST_TOO_LARGE`; a body that is not a JSON object is a 400 `INVALID_JSON`.
- A 503 `QUEUE_FULL` with `Retry-After: 1` once `OLLAYA_MAX_QUEUE` requests wait; a loaded model answers one request at a time, and requests to it queue. The client retries a 503 and honours `Retry-After`.
- Probabilities, confidences and scores are rounded to four decimals.
- `laya` is a router: the response's `model` names the checkpoint that answered (`laya:en`), not the name requested. The hosted API also answers with a version rather than the alias.
- Models are pulled from Ollaya's registry (`ollaya.dev` by default) and never as a side effect of a request.

## What is still open

The run shows the wire, not the model: accuracy and calibration on real cases are not measured here, and Ollaya's own page puts the base `laya:en` near chance zero-shot on typed decisions (0.357). Other models were not run: `winnow:e4b`, which needs an NVIDIA GPU, and `laya:multilingual`, with a 1,024-token context and about 250 options. The profile's pins are expected to hold for them, since none depends on the model's budget, but that is untested. A 503 was not drawn, nor a 413.

## How to repeat it

```sh
# Ollaya 0.17.0, no service, no GPU libraries; zstd unpacks the archive
curl -fsSL https://ollaya.dev/install.sh -o install.sh   # read it first
OLLAYA_VERSION=0.17.0 OLLAYA_NO_SERVICE=1 OLLAYA_INSTALL_DIR=$HOME/.local sh install.sh
ollaya serve &
ollaya pull laya:en
mise run live:ollaya

# with a key, which also runs the bearer test
OLLAYA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11436 OLLAYA_API_KEY=live-secret ollaya serve &
OLLAYA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11436 OLLAYA_API_KEY=live-secret mise run live:ollaya

# a probe by hand: 130 options against laya:en's budget
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11435/v1/systemone -d "{\"model\": \"laya:en\", \"state\": \"Pick one.\",
  \"questions\": {\"c\": {\"type\": \"choice\", \"instructions\": \"Which?\", \"criteria\":
  $(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.dumps({f"o{i}": f"option {i}" for i in range(130)}))')}}}"
```

`OLLAYA_URL` and `OLLAYA_MODEL` point the task at another server or model; it checks that the model is pulled before the suite runs.


<!-- source: docs/project/research/system-one-client-libraries.md -->


# System One client libraries

This is the survey of 2026-09-25 that shaped judgment 0.2; its versions, download counts and line counts are of that date. The field as of 2026-10-04, read again against the released crate and measured, is in [Compared with the other Rust clients](client-comparison.md).

The `judgment` crate was designed in one repository against one consumer. Between 2026-09-16 and 2026-09-25 about twenty-five other Rust crates for the same wire appeared on crates.io, TypeSafe's Python SDK reached 0.7.1, and a live OpenAPI document turned out to exist. Before spending more on the crate it is worth knowing what the field converged on, where judgment is ahead, and where it is behind. This page is that survey: every crate's source was read, not its README, and every claim about the official API was checked against the SDK reference or the OpenAPI document on 2026-09-25.

The headline: the crate's architecture is confirmed, not contradicted. Three independent authors arrived at the same shape as judgment, typed keys that fix an answer's type, a backend trait with a fake behind it, and record-and-replay keyed by request content. What the field has that judgment lacks is wire hardening and parity with the official SDK: a request id on responses and errors, tolerance for answer kinds that do not exist yet, a contract test against the published schema, and the retry details the SDK documents. None of that is a reorientation. It is a 0.2, and it shipped as judgment 0.2.0 on 2026-09-25: [What shipped in judgment 0.2.0](#what-shipped-in-judgment-020) says how each ranked item landed.

Sources: the crates listed below, downloaded from crates.io; [the Python SDK reference](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python/api.md) and [usage guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python/usage.md), [the JavaScript SDK reference](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript/api.md), [the HTTP API page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md); and `https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json`, version 0.2.0. This page covers only the clients, not the models.

## The field

None of the Rust crates is official. TypeSafe's [SDK page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk.md) lists Python and JavaScript only. One crate, `typesafe-io`, declares the official organisation's repository and a documentation page as its home; the crate is owned by an individual account, the documentation page does not exist, and the crate has no retries and no user agent. Treat the claim as false.

The crates fall into five groups. Sizes are lines of Rust including tests; downloads are crates.io totals on 2026-09-25.

| Crate | Lines (approx.) | Downloads | What it is | The one idea worth knowing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `typesafe-sdk-rust` (zchee) | 22,700 | 36 | A port of Python SDK 0.7.1 on hyper, 40% tests | Escapes and truncates every server string before it can reach a log; a tower `Service` transport so a recorder or proxy can sit under the retries |
| `typesafe-client` (JedimEmO) | 6,900 | 59 | Typed keys and a `SystemOne` trait, the closest in spirit to judgment | Verifies the whole response against the questions before returning it, and tests its types against the vendored OpenAPI document |
| `kunobi-jev` | 4,900 | 555 | The most downloaded; typed keys, per-call builder | A total timeout budget that shrinks each attempt and skips a retry that cannot fit; a credential provider asked per attempt; `Answer::Unknown` |
| `typesafe-ai-sdk` (aoprisan) | 5,100 | 93 | SDK port with eleven examples and a REPL | Record and replay as "cassettes" keyed by the SHA-256 of the exact request body |
| `typesafeai-sdk-community` | 10,900 | 74 | The largest feature set | A batch runner whose shared pacer pauses every task on one 429; a check that every backticked path in a question resolves in the state |
| `typesafe-rs` (AbdelStark) | 4,000 | 22 | A `Backend` trait and OpenTelemetry-style span fields | A `conservative()` retry preset that does not retry 5xx or timeouts, because a retried POST is billed twice |
| `system-one` (heyaozh) | 3,700 | 14 | Backend-agnostic with derive macros | A `Shadow` backend that sends every request to two backends and records both; `Replay::with_fallback`; a calibration report |
| `systemone` (lu-zero) | 1,000 | 15 | Executor-agnostic on isahc | Choice option descriptions read from the enum's doc comments, by proc macro or by facet reflection |
| `jev` (porky11) | 1,400 | 118 | Blocking client for hosted and self-hosted backends | A `Verdict::{Yes, Unsure, No}` view on a Noul; a documented evaluation of four backends |
| `typesafe-jev` | 1,900 | 36 | Synchronous on ureq | An additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease concurrency limiter that halves on 429 or 529 |
| the `typesafe-sdk-*` workspace (douglance) | 3,000 | ~200 each | Ten crates for one client | A real-socket test that the timeout covers a stalled body; environment read only through an injected `Process` |
| `jev-rs`, `jev-bridge`, `zev-rs`, `jigor-cli` | 1,600 to 8,600 | 19 to 102 | Servers and bridges: the wire over a stock model's logprobs, an OpenAI-compatible API, a lexical scorer, local ONNX | Wire extensions: an OpenAI-shaped model list, a `debug` block, abstention sentinels, an `uncertainty` block, a `temperature` field, answers without `usage` |
| `fuzzy-jev` | 5,400 | 44 | Jev through OpenRouter's decisions endpoint | The same request body at a different host; the response adds `id`, `provider` and `usage.cost` |

Eleven more (`jev-sdk`, `typesafe-systemone`, `jevlin`, `typesafeai-sdk`, `typesafe-sdk`, `typesafe-rust-sdk`, `typesafe-ai-client`, `typesafe-api`, `sysone`, `gaise-provider-typesafe`, `a3s-apofasi`) are thin ports or wrappers whose one idea, where there is one, appears in the rankings below.

Two facts about the population as a whole. Every crate that took the job seriously converged on the same three things judgment has: a typed key or handle that fixes the answer type (`typesafe-client`, `kunobi-jev`, `jevlin`), a trait over the wire with a scripted fake behind it (`typesafe-client`, `kunobi-jev`, `typesafe-rs`, `system-one`, `typesafe-jev`), and replay keyed by a hash of the request (`typesafe-ai-sdk`, `system-one`). Nobody has what judgment has in its `Observer` seam, its validated `Probability` and `Confidence` newtypes that refuse a bad value on deserialisation, its evaluation module wired to recordings, or a benchmark replay against a second implementation of the wire. Those are the parts to keep.

## What the official sources say that the crate does not know

This section and the ranking below describe judgment 0.1.0, the crate as it was surveyed; "the crate" means that release. What 0.2.0 changed is in [its own section](#what-shipped-in-judgment-020).

The OpenAPI document at `api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json` is version 0.2.0, describes `POST /v1/systemone` and `GET /v1/models`, and is identical to the copy `typesafe-client` vendored on 2026-09-16. It settles several things the crate's rustdoc guesses at:

- `GET /v1/models` is documented, with `ModelMetadata{name, description, release_date}`. The crate's note that the endpoint is "observed rather than documented" is wrong for the OpenAPI document, though the HTTP API page still omits it.
- A Score level is a string, an object or an array, never null; the legend maps a level number to that same value. The fix made in [the Laya run](../verification/laya-typed-decisions.md) is what the schema says. A Choice description may be null.
- `instructions` is optional on every question type; the crate requires it. Score `criteria` has `minItems: 1`; the crate requires two, as the guidance recommends.
- A 422 body is FastAPI's `{"detail": [{"loc", "msg", "type"}]}`. The crate keeps the body as text; it could name the field.
- Nothing about 429, 529, `Retry-After` or a request id header is in the schema. Those are SDK behaviour, documented in the SDK reference and observed by every port.

The Python SDK reference, 0.7.1, fixes the client behaviour the crate claims to mirror:

- **Request id.** Every response and every API error carries `x-typesafe-request-id`. The exception carries status, body, headers, the endpoint without credentials and that id. The crate carries none of them, which is the first thing a support ticket asks for.
- **Retry budget.** The policy has a `timeout` of 30 s per call, "including the initial attempt and delays", and "stops before a retry whose delay would reach or exceed the budget". Jitter is subtracted, never added. `Retry-After` and `retry-after-ms` are both honoured. The crate has no budget, symmetric jitter and reads delay-seconds only; its rustdoc documents each as a deviation, so the claim of SDK parity is a half-truth that should become either parity or a stated policy.
- **Tolerance.** An answer whose `type` the SDK does not know is logged and skipped; `usage` fields are optional, "None when the API did not report it"; unknown fields are ignored. The crate, as of 0.1, fails the whole response on an unknown answer kind and requires `usage`. Every non-TypeSafe server in the survey exercised at least one of those: jigor returns no `usage`, zev adds answer fields, Laya adds three.
- **Escape hatches.** Per-call `model`, `retry`, `timeout`, `extra_headers` and `extra_body` (shallow-merged, for fields such as `beam_width`), and `response_model` for a typed struct of answers. The crate has none of the per-call overrides and no way to send a field it does not know.
- **Key hygiene.** The key is trimmed; an empty key, one with internal whitespace, control or non-ASCII characters is rejected before any request; an explicit empty key does not fall back to the environment. The crate filters blank keys and reports a bad one as a URL error.
- **Gateways.** OpenRouter (`https://openrouter.ai/api`, model `~typesafe/jev-latest`) and Vercel's AI gateway (`https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/typesafe`, model `typesafe-ai/jev`) are documented `base_url` targets. `fuzzy-jev` shows OpenRouter's response adds `id`, `provider` and `usage.cost`, so the tolerance above is what makes a gateway work. (Correction, 2026-10-09: it was not enough. This client dropped the last segment of a base URL's path, so both gateways' base URLs reached `/v1/systemone` at the host's root; the client now keeps the path, [Configure a backend](../../guides/configure-a-backend.md#jev-through-openrouter).)
- **Confidence.** The reference gives the Choice confidence formula as approximately `(n·pmax − 1)/(n − 1)`, marked as a demonstration, and says a Noul has none. Useful for a `Fake` that wants realistic confidences; not a contract.

## Ranked: what to change in judgment

Each item names where the idea was seen, why it matters to this project, and the cost. The order is value per line of code.

1. **Carry the request id.** `x-typesafe-request-id` on `Response`, on `Error::Http`, `RateLimited`, `Overloaded`, `InvalidRequest` and `Unauthorized`, and as a field on the client span. Seen in the official SDK and six crates. Cost: one header read in the retry loop, one field on the completed-response type. Do it first.
2. **Decode tolerantly, validate strictly.** An unknown answer `type` becomes `Answer::Unknown(Value)` with a warning rather than a failed response, the known variants stay strict (kunobi's custom `Deserialize` is the pattern); `usage` and its fields default to zero when absent; unknown top-level fields are kept in a map so an operator can log Laya's `routing` or OpenRouter's `provider`. Seen in the SDK, kunobi, typesafe-rs, fuzzy-jev. Cost: small in code, but not additive: `Answer` was an exhaustive public enum, and under [Cargo's SemVer rules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#enum-variant-new) a new variant on one is a major change, since a consumer's exhaustive `match` stops compiling. The same release should make the enum `#[non_exhaustive]` so the next kind is not.
3. **Verify the response against the questions before returning it.** Every question id answered, every answer of the kind its question asked, every Choice key one of the options sent, every Score legend the levels sent. `typesafe-client` does this in the transport; judgment checks per handle, late, and only for the handles the caller reads. The same check makes `Fake` refuse a scripted answer that does not fit its question, which kunobi's fake does and which catches stale tests. Cost: one pass over the response, about sixty lines, and `Error::AnswerTypeMismatch` gains a sibling for an option outside the question.
4. **Test against the OpenAPI document.** Vendor `openapi.json`, validate every request the builders produce and every response the `Fake` and the committed recordings hold against its schemas with a JSON Schema crate in dev-dependencies, and add an ignored live test that the vendored copy still matches the URL. This is what `typesafe-client` does for this wire. Cost: one dev-dependency, one test file, a copied JSON file.
5. **Retry parity, stated.** Add `retry-after-ms` and HTTP-date `Retry-After` under the existing cap, make jitter one-sided, and add an optional total budget that skips a retry that cannot fit, off by default so no consumer's timing changes. Then the rustdoc can say which of the SDK's behaviours the crate matches and which it declines, rather than "mirrors" with footnotes. `typesafe-rs`'s `conservative()` preset, which does not retry 5xx because a retried POST is billed twice, is worth offering as a named policy for callers who prefer a failed triage to a doubled bill. Cost: medium, all in `http.rs`.
6. **Per-call overrides and an extra body.** `model`, `timeout` and `retry` per request, and a flattened map of extra fields on `Request`, plus extra headers on the builder. The official SDK has all of them; jev-rs's `debug` block and zev's `temperature` are what a consumer would put there. Cost: small; `Request` grows three optional fields.
7. **Fix the small things the schema shows.** `instructions` optional; 400 classified as `InvalidRequest` alongside 422 and 403 as its own variant, since jev-bridge returns 400 for a bad body; a dedicated `Error::InvalidApiKey` with the SDK's hygiene rules; parse the 422 `detail` list into field paths; correct the `/v1/models` note. Cost: trivial each.
8. **Distribution helpers as pure functions.** `ranked()`, `margin()` between the top two, `top(n)` on a Choice; `probability_at_least(level)` on a Score; the probability of the reported answer as a method rather than a lookup. Seen in kunobi, typesafeai-sdk-community, typesafe-rust-sdk, jev. They are pure, they cost nothing, and the benchmark example and every consumer's policy re-derive them by hand. jev-bridge's finding that order flips cluster where the top-two margin is at or below 0.24 is the kind of rule a policy wants `margin()` for. Cost: trivial. What stays out: a `decide(min_confidence)` that returns an option, a three-band verdict, a cost-matrix decision. Those are policy, and decisions 0002 and 0008 keep policy in the application.
9. **Expose backend limits as data.** Maximum options, maximum levels and a context budget on the backend, so a caller can shortlist before the wire and the harness can report a refusal as a gap. The small open models cap options at 16 to 26; jev-bridge at 16; zev serves `/v1/limits`. Cost: a `Limits` value with a default for TypeSafe's 255 and 10, a method on the trait with a default implementation.
10. **A `Shadow` backend.** Send each request to two backends, return the first, record both. `system-one` has it; the Jev-versus-Laya comparison the roadmap wants is exactly this, and the evaluation harness would get paired requests for free. Cost: about eighty lines on top of `Recorder`.
11. **Order-flip rate in `eval`.** Rotate or reverse the option order and count changed answers; jev-rs averages rotations, jev-bridge measures the flip rate and found a real position bias on the reference endpoint. A `Replay` cannot do this, only a live run can, so it belongs beside the live tests. Cost: medium.
12. **Concurrency control.** A semaphore on the client (kunobi) or an AIMD pacer that halves on 429 (typesafe-jev, the community batch runner). A consumer that answers one request at a time has no use for it; the day one replays history in bulk or serves a burst, this is the first thing it needs. Cost: small for the semaphore, medium for the pacer. Wait for the need.

## Rejected, and why

- **Ten crates for one client** (the douglance workspace). The split buys nothing at three thousand lines and costs a release dance for every change. judgment's feature flag already separates the questions from the transport.
- **A cache of probabilistic answers** keyed by request (community SDK). A cached judgment is a stale judgment with a fresh timestamp; `Replay` exists for the one legitimate use, tests, and says so in its name.
- **Policy in the wire crate**: cost-matrix `decide`, entropy-based gates, sampling from the distribution (`system-one`, `jev`). Decision 0002 puts thresholds in code the application owns and tunes; a helper that hides the threshold moves it into a dependency.
- **A synchronous client.** Five crates ship one; no consumer here has asked, and blocking on the future costs one line.
- **Untagged, dual-dialect answer parsing** (`jev`), which accepts answers without a `type`. Item 2 keeps unknown kinds without loosening the known ones; a server that omits `type` (jigor guesses the kind from the fields) is outside the schema and should be fixed there.
- **Cassette compatibility with `typesafe-ai-sdk`**, whose key is the SHA-256 of the exact request body. judgment's key is a 64-bit hash of the canonical, key-sorted JSON, so two clients that serialise questions in a different order share a recording. The formats are documented on both sides; converting is a script, not a feature.
- **Reading option descriptions from doc comments** (`systemone`). Charming, and it ties the API contract to rustdoc formatting; `options!` keeps the description next to the key where a reviewer looks for it.
- **The `secrecy` crate for the key.** judgment redacts `Debug` and never logs the key; zeroising memory guards against a threat this deployment does not have.

## What to do with this
